Overview

Evidence cut-off 2026-11-04, · Scope: Chapter 2 (Freedom of movement for workers) and Technology and AI recommendations; comparator step on three issues

Overall assessment Agent synthesis, validated at G7

This overview lists the 53 reform issues identified for Moldova in RUN-2026-02: 16 under Chapter 2 (Freedom of movement for workers) and 37 under the cross-cutting technology and AI theme. All values shown are judgements validated by the analyst at G6. Seventeen issues are rated High priority (3 in Chapter 2 and 14 in the technology theme), 24 Medium and 12 Low. The three High priority Chapter 2 issues are the framework for joining EURES, gaps in bilateral social security and healthcare agreements, and the missing domestic preconditions for the European Health Insurance Card. The dominant pattern is improvement: 28 of 53 issues have an improving direction of travel, 15 are persistent, one is new (host-language tuition for EU workers and their children, which is not raised in EU material) and 9 cannot be judged on the evidence. Five High priority issues are persistent: the European Health Insurance Card preconditions, digital communication with the courts, the independence and resources of the data protection authority, the security of 5G networks and the outdated electronic procurement system. Where an improvement is in law only, the issue briefs say so. No issue's gap is closed: 16 gaps are open, 33 partly addressed and 4 cannot be judged. Most issues are of Medium tractability (35), 13 are High, 2 are Low and 3 cannot be judged. The comparator step covered three High priority issues: the European Health Insurance Card preconditions (RI-FMW-015), the outdated electronic procurement system (RI-TEC-038) and the national e-services portal (RI-TEC-036).

RI-FMW-015 · Moldova

Domestic preconditions for the European Health Insurance Card not in place

Chapter 2

The country has no national health insurance card or integrated health information system, so it cannot yet issue or accept the European Health Insurance Card at accession.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
■Unresolved gap Open Validated
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to develop the IT infrastructure, systems, capacity and resources needed for full participation in the European Health Insurance Card scheme, and it has found in each report from 2023 to 2025 that no national health insurance card exists because there is no integrated health information system. The National Health Insurance Company coordinates the work, and a feasibility study on the financial impact of the card was finalised in August 2026, when an EHIC Action Plan was also approved as a roadmap. The feasibility study is the only step assessed as implemented. The card module in the health insurance information system is being developed, the amendments to the health care and health insurance laws are planned for 2026, and the order on the card's technical specifications is a draft, none of them shown adopted or in operation. The Government states that the EU acts on the card are not yet transposed, and the Commission found in 2024 that an integrated health information system is not yet in place. No card has been issued. What remains is a national health insurance card and the IT, legal and administrative basis to issue and accept the European Health Insurance Card at accession. The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    12 EU requirement items, 2023 to 2026.

    The Commission's analytical report of February 2023 found that no national health insurance card exists because there is no integrated health information system, and that implementing the European Health Insurance Card might be challenging. The 2023 and 2024 reports repeat both findings in the same words. The 2024 report also recommended implementing the national health strategy, including an integrated e-health system. The 2025 report records no progress on the card, repeats the finding on the national card and adds a key recommendation to develop IT infrastructure for the card. The 2026 report widens this to the measures, capacity, resources and IT systems needed for full participation in the scheme, alongside EURES and EESSI, and reports the feasibility study and action plan.   5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ■Unresolved gap Open Validated

    The 2025 and 2026 key recommendations still require IT infrastructure, systems and capacity for the EHIC scheme. Only the feasibility study is implemented: the EHIC module in the health insurance information system, the amendments to the health care and health insurance laws, the technical specifications of the card and the integrated health information system are planned or under development, and the Government states that the EU acts on the card are not yet transposed (machine translated). What remains is a national health insurance card and the IT, legal and administrative basis to issue and accept the European Health Insurance Card at accession.

    →Direction of travel Persistent Validated

    Sub-area wording on the European Health Insurance Card, which matches this issue, records no progress in 2025, and the finding that no national health insurance card exists because there is no integrated health information system is unchanged in the 2023 report, the 2023 Analytical Report and the 2024 and 2025 reports. In 2026 the Commission reports a finalised feasibility study and an approved EHIC Action Plan, which are planning steps and do not yet show a change in the card or the health information system.

  6. Comparator evidence Stated
    CMP-0010

    Croatia

    What was done: Croatia prepared the European Health Insurance Card before its accession on 1 July 2013: a regulation on the card was adopted in December 2011, the Commission found preparations reaching completion in October 2012, and the Croatian Health Insurance Fund (HZZO) reports issuing the card in 2013 and EU visitors using it. Croatia already had a central health information system (CEZIH), migrated to new hardware in 2012, and by 2013 HZZO was issuing national health insurance cards alongside the EHIC, so the case shows the end state Moldova is working towards rather than how to build the missing preconditions. All statements of results come from HZZO's own reports.

    Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Croatia shows the end state that Moldova's preparations aim at, with the health insurer issuing both the national card and the EHIC by 2013, working from a central health information system, and a secondary act fixing the card's validity, form and issuing details about 18 months before accession. Moldova's draft CNAM order on the card's technical specifications and the provisional replacement certificate is the nearest counterpart of Croatia's 2011 regulation. The case does not show how to build a national card or an integrated health information system where none exists, which is Moldova's gap.

    ◆Comparator relevance Medium Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

    No evidence recorded for this step in this run.

    CMP-0011

    Montenegro

    What was done: Montenegro recognises the European Health Insurance Card in its Law on compulsory health insurance but will introduce it only after accession, in wording the Commission repeats in 2024, 2025 and 2026. Asked in 2025 for a feasibility study, it updated one with 2025 data and in February 2026 adopted an action plan for social security coordination that sets out the technical and IT upgrades needed before accession. Chapter 2 was provisionally closed in June 2026, but no source in the project links the closure to the card, the card has not been issued and the Commission still asks for the health information system to be adapted.

    Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Montenegro is some months ahead of Moldova on the same route, a feasibility study on public finances followed by an action plan that carries its findings; Moldova finalised its study and approved its EHIC Action Plan in August 2026. Once those were in place, the Commission's request to Montenegro became concrete: adapt the health information system for the card, equip the insurer and budget for reimbursements by accession. Moldova faces the same tasks with the added one of building an integrated system Montenegro already has. Montenegro had also recognised the card in its health insurance law before the chapter closed, while Moldova plans its law amendments for 2026; the case does not show that this recognition, or deferring the card to accession, was what the EU required.

    ▲Comparator relevance High Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

    No evidence recorded for this step in this run.

    CMP-0012

    Serbia

    What was done: Serbia is a contrast case: the Commission recorded no developments on the European Health Insurance Card, in identical words, in its 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports, and in 2025 and 2026 asked Serbia in a key recommendation to develop the IT infrastructure for the card. No Serbian measure on the card's domestic preconditions appears in the evidence, and no source says why the position has not moved.

    Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Serbia received nearly the same recommendation as Moldova in 2025, and the Commission recorded no developments in 2024, 2025 and 2026, including in the year after that recommendation, with no feasibility study or plan visible in the evidence. Moldova has already gone further, with a feasibility study and an EHIC Action Plan in August 2026, so the contrast mainly shows what the Commission records when such steps are missing. It offers no lesson on the causes of a stall.

    ▽Comparator relevance Low Validated ∅Transferability Insufficient evidence Validated

  7. Lesson Assessed

    Three points recur. First, once a feasibility study and a plan exist, the Commission's request becomes concrete. After Montenegro's updated study and its February 2026 action plan, the Commission asked it to adapt its health information system for the card, equip its Health Insurance Fund and budget for reimbursements, all by accession. Moldova reached the same point in August 2026, when it finalised its feasibility study and approved an EHIC Action Plan, so the same three tasks are likely to follow, with the added task of building the integrated system that Montenegro already has. Second, legal recognition is not delivery. Montenegro recognises the card in its health insurance law but will introduce it only after accession, and the Commission still asks for its preconditions after the chapter was provisionally closed; whether the EU would accept such a deferral for Moldova cannot be judged from the evidence. Third, a recommendation alone did not move the position in Serbia: the Commission recorded no developments on the card in 2024, 2025 and 2026, including in the year after a key recommendation worded almost as Moldova's. Croatia adds that a secondary act fixing the card's validity, form and issuing was adopted about 18 months before accession, and that its insurer saw preparing contracted providers to treat visitors as the main test at accession. Agent synthesis, validated at G6b

    No evidence recorded for this step in this run.

    Option 1: Set the national health insurance card and the integrated health information system as dated, budgeted steps that come before the card itself

    Details
    Comparator it draws on
    Croatia, Montenegro
    Gap it addresses
    the missing national health insurance card and integrated health information system, without which Moldova cannot issue or accept the European Health Insurance Card.
    Rationale
    Croatia (relevance Medium) shows the end state, with its insurer issuing the national card and the European card together by 2013 from a central health information system. Montenegro (relevance High) shows that, after the study and the plan, the Commission's next request is to adapt the information system, equip the insurer and budget for reimbursements.
    Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
    Conditional: both countries had the foundations Moldova lacks, so neither case shows how to build them, only that they come first.
    Problem it targets
    weak administrative capacity (MEC-03) and insufficient resources (MEC-09).
    Preconditions
    the content of Moldova's EHIC Action Plan, which the evidence describes only as a roadmap for operational implementation; a decision on how the card module under development in the health insurance information system relates to the wider integrated system.
    Risks
    building a card module before the national system it depends on; a plan that sets steps without a budget, given that the work depends on external and national funds.
    Responsible actor
    the Government, which the Commission has asked since 2024 to develop an integrated e-health system, with the National Health Insurance Company (CNAM), which coordinates the card.

RI-TEC-010 · Moldova

Digital communication with courts and justice system connections incomplete

Technology and AI Digitalisation of government or economic activity Digital government and digital public services

Digital communication with courts is incomplete, or justice system IT does not connect between institutions.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
■Unresolved gap Open Validated
▲Priority High Validated
▽Tractability Low Validated

The EU asks Moldova to digitalise its justice system and connect the IT systems of justice institutions. The Reform Agenda requires, by December 2027, the E-File application to be operational in all first instance courts with at least 15 percent of cases processed through it, and the integrated case management system to cover all cases and connect with seven information systems; a 2026 key recommendation asks for substantial progress on an integrated electronic case management system for law enforcement and prosecution bodies. Moldova set up an Agency for Digitalisation in Justice and Judicial Administration on 1 January 2025, with a mandate for the development and interoperability of justice sector information systems, and in August 2026 made normative amendments promoting the digitalisation of certain judicial procedures. What has happened in practice is limited: the Commission finds that the Agency has an extremely limited capacity because of persistent staffing concerns and that the use of IT tools across the justice system remains uneven and partial. No source reports progress on the E-File application. What remains is digital communication with courts in practice and connected IT across justice institutions, run by an agency able to deliver it. The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is High and tractability is Low. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    6 EU requirement items, 2024 to 2026.

    The evidence holds no Commission item on justice digitalisation from the 2022 Opinion or the 2023 report. The 2024 report stated in general terms that digitalisation of the justice system needs to be improved. In 2025 the Commission recorded the new Agency and asked for its operationalisation to be sped up, and the Reform Agenda of the same year set concrete, dated targets for the E-File application and the integrated case management system. By 2026 the Commission's wording had become more specific and more critical: it found the Agency's capacity extremely limited and IT use uneven and partial, called for further legal improvements and a decisive reinforcement of the Agency's mandate and capacity, and made an integrated case management system for law enforcement and prosecution bodies a key recommendation. The August 2026 amendments are recorded but not yet assessed. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

The Agency exists but has extremely limited capacity, the August 2026 amendments are adopted, and the E-File application, which the Reform Agenda requires in all first instance courts by December 2027, is still planned. What remains is digital communication with courts in practice and connected IT across justice institutions, run by an agency able to deliver it.

    →Direction of travel Persistent Validated

    The chapter scale was not decisive, since this issue concerns only part of Chapter 23. The 2024 report says justice digitalisation needs to improve, the 2025 report that the new Agency for Digitalisation in Justice needs faster operationalisation, and the 2026 report finds the Agency's capacity extremely limited and the use of IT tools across the justice system uneven and partial. The August 2026 amendments promoting digitalisation of some judicial procedures are recorded but not yet assessed.

Technology and AI Data and data governance

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to increase the capacity of its data protection supervisory authority, the National Centre for Personal Data Protection, especially its staff. Moldova adopted Law No. 195/2024 on personal data protection, which entered into force in August 2026, widens the authority's mandate and creates a data protection inspector function. Strengthening the authority's administrative capacity, especially its human resources, is set as an objective for 2026 but has not yet been carried out. No increase in capacity is shown. The Commission found 39 staff for 45 posts in 2023, and the authority reports 36 staff at the end of 2025, nine short of its limit, with a staff turnover rate of 18%. In 2026 the Commission found that the authority's human, technical and financial capacities had not grown with its expanded mandate. In its own account, the authority reports pay below comparable supervisory bodies, too few staff in its surveillance and legal departments, and pressure, intimidation and abusive challenges against its staff without adequate safeguards. What remains is to give the authority the staff, pay, budget and safeguards it needs to supervise independently under the new law. The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-024 · Moldova

Security of 5G networks not ensured

Technology and AI Cybersecurity Digital infrastructure and connectivity

The EU 5G Cybersecurity Toolbox, including supplier risk assessment and restrictions on high-risk suppliers, is not fully transposed or applied when 5G networks are deployed.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
■Unresolved gap Open Validated
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to implement the EU 5G Cybersecurity Toolbox, including assessing the risk profile of suppliers and putting in place restrictions or exclusions for high-risk suppliers. The Reform Agenda sets full alignment by December 2027 as a step: a legal framework, an assessment of assets and suppliers, and restrictions on high-risk suppliers for critical and highly sensitive assets. Moldova has started preparatory work. A grant agreement with Swedfund, approved in March 2025, funds a study of the impact and risks of the Toolbox, and in October 2025 the ministry contracted KPMG AB for a supplier risk assessment, recommendations on restricting high-risk suppliers, cost estimates, an operator compensation mechanism and a draft law. In April 2026 the Government reported the study still under way and a draft act on 5G network security still being finalised. The Commission's 2026 report records secondary legislation on the security of public 5G networks among Moldova's steps to align with the NIS 2 Directive. A law on 5G network cybersecurity is planned by December 2027. No source shows a supplier assessment completed or any restriction applied. The Government notes that compliance requires major investment in 5G networks. What remains is the 5G security law, the completed supplier risk assessment and restrictions on high-risk suppliers applied to critical assets. The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-038 · Moldova

Electronic public procurement system outdated and in need of replacement

Technology and AI Digital government and digital public services

The electronic public procurement system is outdated or functionally inadequate: it does not support all procedures, tools or stages of the procurement cycle set out in law, hampers centralised procurement, and has to be re-engineered or replaced by a new system.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
■Unresolved gap Open Validated Flagged for re-review
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to finalise the development of a new electronic procurement system and make it operational, and the Reform Agenda sets as a payment condition a pilot of the new system, with eTendering, eAwarding, eInvoicing, eComplaint and e-catalogues, by December 2027. The current MTender system, launched in 2018, has enabled electronic procurement and public access to documents, but it lacks annual planning and contract management modules and does not offer all the procedures and award instruments set out in law. Its re-engineering is part of the Government's public procurement development programme 2023-2026, and the Commission reports that development of a new system advanced with funding from international partners. Government monitoring, in machine translation, records that technical specifications were received in September 2025, tender documents went to the World Bank in October 2025, and the tender to develop the new system was published in December 2025 with bids due on 10 February 2026. The new system has not yet been built, and no outcome has been assessed. In 2026 the Commission still found the outdated MTender limiting the procurement agency's monitoring, since delivery, invoices, payments, amendments and performance are not captured digitally. What remains is designing, building and putting into operation a new system that covers every procedure and stage of the procurement cycle. The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

Montenegro's response was an independent diagnostic requested by the procurement policy body, which was then used to secure EU funds for an upgrade; whether the upgrade worked is not known.

  7. Lesson Assessed

    Two points recur. First, a new system can itself become the problem. Montenegro's system was under implementation from January 2021, and an independent World Bank assessment, requested by the national procurement policy body, found in 2023 that it was a good start but needed substantial upgrading and that old technology limited further upgrading. The assessment's findings were then used to secure EU funds for an upgrade, but the only stated effect since is the Commission's unmeasured sentence on improved monitoring functions. Moldova received the technical specifications for its new system in September 2025 and published the call for bids in December 2025, so its technology choice is being made now. Second, a working system follows the law and grows in stages. North Macedonia's system was adapted to its new procurement law and modules were added over several years, under one responsible body, and its use is obligatory for all contracting authorities; this is the state Moldova is aiming for, not the route to it. Moldova's own problem is that MTender does not allow all the tools in its law and lacks annual planning and contract management, and contract management is not among the stages listed for North Macedonia either, so neither case gives evidence on it.     Problem it targets
    weak administrative capacity (MEC-03) and insufficient resources (MEC-09), since the system depends on funding from international partners.
    Preconditions
    a map of every procedure and stage in Moldova's law against the modules planned, including those beyond the essential modules in the Reform Agenda pilot; a budget for adapting the system after donor funding ends, which neither case shows.
    Risks
    a pilot of essential modules that leaves planning and contract management for later, keeping the alternative solutions that the Commission says may cause delays.
    Responsible actor
    the Centre for Information Technologies in Finance as owner and operator, with the Public Procurement Agency, whose monitoring depends on the data captured.

RI-FMW-004 · Moldova

Legal and organisational framework for joining EURES

Chapter 2

The country has not set up the legal and organisational arrangements needed to join the European network of employment services, such as a system for appointing EURES members and partners and access for private employment agencies.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
▲Tractability High Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to prepare to join the European Network of Employment Services (EURES) upon accession, and in 2025 added that this should include reinforcing the Public Employment Service's IT infrastructure. Moldova has created a Labour Migration and EURES Department in the National Employment Agency, adopted Government Decision No. 617/2024 and Government Decision No. 607/2025 setting the national legal framework, designated the Agency as National Coordination Office and approved a procedure for admitting EURES members and partners. The Commission also reports ten territorial EURES members, implementing acts on data collection and monitoring, and technical standards for matching vacancies and CVs with the EURES portal. These are preparatory steps: no source reports any organisation admitted under the new procedure, and the Government itself describes its decisions as only partial alignment with the EURES Regulation. What remains, on the Government's own account, is better data exchange between the Agency and the European platform and the completion of legislative alignment, with an order on interoperability planned for December 2027. There is no outcome evidence. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is High and tractability is High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-FMW-008 · Moldova

Gaps in bilateral social security and healthcare agreements

Chapter 2

Bilateral social security coordination and healthcare agreements do not yet cover all EU Member States or all branches, so workers moving before accession lack coordinated protection.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

Until accession, workers moving between Moldova and the EU rely on bilateral social security agreements, and the Commission asks Moldova to conclude more of them, in particular with EU Member States. By 2023 Moldova had agreements with 13 Member States and Türkiye. Since then the agreement with Greece entered into force in January 2023, those with Spain and Latvia in June and July 2024, agreements with Italy and France were signed in October 2024 and March 2025, the Italian one entered into force in September 2025 and one with Slovakia was signed in March 2026. The Government states that it has signed agreements with 17 of the 27 Member States. The National Social Insurance House negotiates the agreements and applies them. Signature and entry into force do not show that workers are better protected: the Government's claim of better social protection for Moldovans working abroad is not backed by data on coverage or benefits paid, so success cannot be assessed. The Government also says it cannot commit to a number of agreements because this depends on the political will of other states. What remains is agreements with the Member States not yet covered, entry into force of those signed, and gap analyses on the coordination regulations. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    14 EU requirement items, 2023 to 2026.

    The 2023 analytical report described the existing agreements, noting that they apply the principles of equal treatment and aggregation. The 2023 report asked Moldova to work on concluding additional coordination agreements, notably with Member States, and to step up signing them, and judged progress limited. The 2024 report repeated the recommendation and still found limited progress. In 2025 the Commission found good progress through new agreements, and widened the recommendation to cover IT infrastructure for the European Health Insurance Card and the electronic exchange of social security information. The 2026 report again found good progress, citing the Slovakia agreement, kept the recommendation to conclude more agreements and added a request for gap analyses on the coordination regulations. Each report from 2024 to 2026 says that negotiations with other Member States have been initiated and should continue. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-002 · Moldova

Digital transformation strategy and governance weak

Technology and AI Digitalisation of government or economic activity Digital government and digital public services

There is no adopted long-term strategy for digital transformation aligned with EU targets, or the ministry or agency responsible lacks the capacity, staff and inter-institutional coordination to lead and monitor it.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated Flagged for re-review
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to have a digital transformation strategy and the institutional capacity to implement it. The Digital Transformation Strategy 2023-2030 was adopted in September 2023, a National Council for Digital Transformation was set up in November 2023 to coordinate it, and a programme implementing the strategy for 2025 to 2027 was adopted in May 2025. The Commission reports tangible progress on the strategy's key performance indicators in 2025 and 2026. Earlier experience shows why delivery matters: the expired Digital Moldova 2020 strategy met only 6 of its 12 targets. Capacity remains the weak point. The Government estimates the programme at 613 million lei, of which 225 million lei are uncovered, and states that implementation requires building capacity in the ministry and the e-Governance Agency. It names the lack of centralised coordination of digitalisation initiatives as the main barrier, and a public body consulted on the programme warned that the two bodies are responsible for most of its 68 actions. Government sources also cite low pay for IT staff, scarce resources and staff turnover after reorganisations, and the Court of Accounts found a recommendation on documenting information systems only partly implemented, citing insufficient institutional capacity. What remains is the staff, funding and coordination capacity to deliver and monitor the strategy. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    12 EU requirement items, 2023 to 2026.

    The 2023 report asked Moldova to adopt the Digital Transformation Strategy 2023-2030 and ensure the institutional capacity to implement it, and to set up a National Digital Transformation Council. Once the strategy was adopted, the 2024 key recommendation shifted to ensuring capacity to implement its priority areas, in particular alignment on electronic identification, data protection and cybersecurity, including the 5G Toolbox. The 2025 and 2026 reports keep this wording, asking for capacity to "continue" implementation, with the focus on data protection and cybersecurity standards. Over the same period the Commission's findings moved from some progress in 2024 to good progress in 2025 and 2026, on the strength of progress against the strategy's indicators.     The strategy, the council and an implementation programme are in place, but the Commission repeats in 2024, 2025 and 2026 its key recommendation to ensure institutional capacity to implement the strategy.     ↑Direction of travel Improving Validated

The 2025 report notes an implementation programme for 2025 to 2027 and tangible progress on all key performance indicators, and the 2026 report again records progress on them. The Chapter 10 rating rose from some level of preparation in 2023 to 2025 to moderately prepared in 2026, but it rates the whole chapter and was not decisive.

RI-TEC-009 · Moldova

eHealth systems not interoperable or aligned with EU rules

Technology and AI Digital government and digital public services Interoperability and electronic systems Data and data governance

Electronic health systems are not interoperable with health insurance data, referrals remain on paper, and the legislation is not aligned with the EU acquis on eHealth.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to develop an integrated e-health system with interoperability between all health information systems, and the Reform Agenda requires electronic health records for 40% of the insured population by December 2027. Moldova has adopted the National Programme for Digitalisation and Innovation in Health 2025-2030. An electronic prescription system has operated since April 2024 for reimbursed medicines and devices, and by 2026 it had been modernised and a fully digital system for medical certificates introduced. The Government reports over 270,000 reimbursed prescriptions issued a month at the end of 2024, but this figure is its own. The rest is still planned: a concept, architecture and regulatory framework for the electronic health record by the end of 2026, a draft Government decision on the record still in preparation in 2026, and a decision creating a national e-health entity. The Government itself names the lack of a functional electronic health record, limited interoperability and the absence of a dedicated institutional framework as major challenges, and describes the legal framework as only partially aligned with EU law. What remains is an eHealth legal framework aligned with the EU acquis, an interoperable integrated health information system and electronic health records in use. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    4 EU requirement items, 2023 to 2025.

    The 2023 report found limited progress on an e-health legal framework and no e-health strategy in place. In 2024 the Commission found that an integrated health information system was not yet in place, while noting the new electronic prescription system, and made an integrated e-health system and interoperability of all health information systems part of a key recommendation on the health strategy. The 2025 key recommendation shifted the wording to the digitalisation of health services and the protection of personal data. The Reform Agenda of 2025 stated that Moldova lacked an approved eHealth strategy and regulatory framework, and set conditions for a legal framework followed by electronic health records, a National Contact Point for eHealth by December 2025 and records for 40% of the insured by December 2027. The 2026 report records the new health digitalisation programme and the modernised prescription system rather than a new requirement. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-015 · Moldova

Base registers incomplete, unreliable or not digitalised

Technology and AI Data and data governance Digitalisation of government or economic activity

Key registers, above all the population register, hold data of poor quality or are little used, and many institutional, property and intellectual property registers are not yet digitalised or kept up to date.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The EU asks Moldova to complete the full digitalisation of the public property register, and the Reform Agenda requires a fully operational State Register of Legal Units by December 2025 and a digital cadastre covering 98 percent of the territory, with data regularly updated and online, by December 2027. Moldova digitalised the business register's paper archive between August 2023 and August 2024 and launched the State Register of Legal Units portal on 29 December 2025, with a World Bank loan funding its pilot phase. The Commission judged the related Reform Agenda step satisfactorily fulfilled, and verified that 310 of 414 business services are digitalised, although only 133 are fully digital end to end. The civil status records system went into production on 3 November 2025, but no source reports its use since. Other registers have moved less: the public property register is still being prepared for digitalisation, the State Population Register concept was withdrawn in August 2025 and resumed in 2026, and the register of non-commercial organisations is described as outdated and not interoperable. Sources disagree on whether all state information systems are registered in the register of state information systems. What remains is a fully digital public property register, the planned modernisation of the population register and the cadastre, and reliable data across base registers. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-017 · Moldova

Personal data protection law not aligned with EU rules

Technology and AI Data and data governance

The personal data protection framework is not fully aligned with the General Data Protection Regulation, the Law Enforcement Directive and the ePrivacy Directive, rules on international transfers are missing, and sector laws are not harmonised.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
▲Tractability High Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to align its personal data protection legislation with the General Data Protection Regulation and the Law Enforcement Directive, to ratify the amending protocol to Council of Europe Convention 108 and to adopt rules on standard contractual clauses between controllers and processors. Parliament adopted Law No. 195/2024 on personal data protection on 25 July 2024 to align with the Regulation, and it entered into force in 2026. In May 2026 Moldova ratified the second protocol to Convention 108, and in August 2026 it adopted a law on personal data processed for crime prevention, aligning with the Law Enforcement Directive. No source yet shows either law being applied, and no outcome has been assessed; in 2025 the data protection authority was still preparing guidelines on applying the new law. The order on standard contractual clauses exists only as a draft, and the Commission states in 2026 that Moldova should still implement these standards. The review of related national laws, described in 2023 as pending since 2020 and recommended by the World Bank in 2024, is not reported as completed. What remains is the rules on standard contractual clauses and the alignment of related national laws with the new data protection laws. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is improving, legal only. Priority is High and tractability is High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    16 EU requirement items, 2021 to 2026.

    In 2021 the Commission noted that a draft data protection law had been awaiting its second reading in Parliament since November 2018. The February 2023 analytical report found some laws aligned with the Regulation, eID and ePrivacy rules and called for secondary legislation, including on personal data protection, to be amended. The November 2023 report found the law only to some extent aligned with the Regulation and the Law Enforcement Directive and said implementing legislation needed amending. From 2024 the requirement entered the Chapter 10 key recommendations, as aligning legislation with data protection standards within the capacity to implement the digital strategy, and the 2024 report found the framework not yet aligned with the Law Enforcement Directive. The 2025 report made the requirement specific: alignment with the Law Enforcement Directive, ratification of the Convention 108 protocol and rules on standard contractual clauses, and it also called for better capacity at the data protection authority. By 2026, with two of these met, the key recommendation asks for further alignment and the remaining specific requirement is the contractual clauses. No Reform Agenda payment condition on the issue was found. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-022 · Moldova

Cybersecurity legal and strategic framework incomplete

Technology and AI Cybersecurity

Network and information security law is not fully aligned with the NIS2 Directive and the Cybersecurity Act, the national cybersecurity strategy is late or fragmented in implementation, and responsibilities are split without effective coordination.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated Flagged for re-review

The Commission's key recommendations of 2024, 2025 and 2026 ask Moldova to align its legislation with EU cybersecurity standards, and the Reform Agenda commits it to a law transposing the NIS 2 Directive, with cybersecurity responsibilities clarified. Moldova adopted Law No. 48/2023 on cybersecurity, in force since January 2025, and the Commission records Government decisions implementing it with the aim of NIS 2 alignment, further secondary legislation on cyber incidents and 5G security in 2026, and the National Cybersecurity Programme 2026-2030, adopted in December 2025. The Government itself describes Law No. 48/2023 as only partially harmonising national law with NIS 2, and the amending law for NIS 2, the laws on the Cyber Resilience Act and on cybersecurity certification, and the designation of a market surveillance authority were still planned for 2026 and 2027. Most of the new acts are adopted but not yet shown in application, and no outcome has been assessed. The Cyber Security Agency reports that some of its 2025 work was only partly done because of too few staff and incomplete rules, and the ministry's cybersecurity policy unit has four posts, one vacant. These Government documents are machine translated. What remains is full transposition of NIS 2, the Cyber Resilience Act and the certification framework, with the authorities designated to apply them. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is improving, mainly legal and strategic. Priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    6 EU requirement items, 2023 to 2026.

    In 2021 the Commission's concern was operational: a national computer emergency response team foreseen by the 2019-2024 strategy was still pending approval of its mandate. The February 2023 analytical report said Moldova would need to align with the NIS framework. After the Law on cybersecurity was adopted, the November 2023 report said its implementation had to start. From 2024 the requirement became a standing key recommendation to align legislation with EU cybersecurity standards, including the 5G Cybersecurity Toolbox, repeated in 2025 and, as "further aligning", in 2026. The 2025 Reform Agenda sharpened it: it found no holistic cybersecurity framework and no plans for large-scale incidents, noted that the 2019-2024 strategy had lapsed, and set out a NIS 2 law, clearer institutional roles and mandatory requirements for products in view of the Cyber Resilience Act. It also warned that operators may resist compliance costs. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

The EU asks Moldova to align its law on electronic identification and trust services with EU requirements, now including the European Digital Identity framework (eIDAS 2), and to make its national wallet interoperable with the European Digital Identity Wallets; the Reform Agenda expects eIDAS 2 alignment, an EU-aligned national wallet and at least 20 e-services in the EVO application by December 2026. Moldova adopted Law No. 124/2022 on electronic identification and trust services, amended it in 2025 to open the market to EU qualified trust service providers, and joined the EU Digital Identity Cooperation Group. The Commission reports that December 2025 amendments fully aligned the rules on qualified trust service providers with the Digital Identity Regulation and that Moldova joined the EU third country trusted list for advanced electronic signatures and seals. A first national wallet was launched in the EVO application in June 2024, and work on a wallet aligned with the EU framework began in September 2025. The law transposing eIDAS 2 is still being drafted, and implementing orders on registering wallet-relying parties and certifying wallets are planned for December 2026. Capacity is thin, with one ministry employee covering information technology, information society and trust services. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is improving, legal only. Priority is High and tractability is High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-026 · Moldova

Electronic identification and trust services not usable or recognised

Technology and AI Digital identity

Electronic identification and signature tools are costly, cumbersome and little used, qualified trust services are not widely available, and the country is not yet on the EU trusted list or in cross-border wallet arrangements.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asked Moldova to join the third-country trusted list as a first step towards mutual recognition of qualified trust services and to make its wallet interoperable with the European Digital Identity Wallets, and a Reform Agenda payment condition due in December 2026 requires an EU-aligned EVO Sign, membership of the trusted list, eIDAS 2 alignment and 20 e-services in EVO. The Government reports that Law No. 117/2025 opened the market to EU qualified trust service providers, and the Commission reports that amendments of December 2025 fully aligned the rules on qualified trust service providers and that Moldova joined the EU third-country trusted list. The sources conflict on the related draft law: the Commission reports full alignment in December 2025, while the Government's 2025 progress report still describes the draft as being prepared. They also conflict on EVOSign: the Commission reports it launched and the ministry says it is officially available, while other public bodies say it is still at the pilot stage and lacks the confirmations needed for use. New identity cards with a qualified signature have been issued since March 2025, one million of them in 2025, though no source shows how often the signature is used. The EU-aligned wallet was started only in September 2025, its cross-border interoperability has been tested, and remote identification has moved to 2027. Use has barely moved: the Commission gives 200 000 electronic signature users, 9.8% of adults, in 2024 and over 266 000, 10%, in 2025, and civil society reports fees of at least 11 euros a year. What remains is a working EU-aligned wallet, mutual recognition in practice and much wider, cheaper use of electronic identification and signatures. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is High and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-029 · Moldova

Customs IT systems not aligned with EU electronic customs

Technology and AI Interoperability and electronic systems

National customs IT systems are not yet aligned with the EU electronic customs strategic plan, and upgrades such as the New Computerised Transit System phases, export and import control systems are delayed or understaffed.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
▲Tractability High Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to build customs IT systems that enable a fully digital customs environment interoperable with the EU, to adopt Customs Code amendments that give these systems a legal basis, and to advance its customs IT programme, prioritising core interconnectivity systems and a single window. Moldova migrated nationwide to Phase 5 of the New Computerised Transit System in October 2024 and completed the Phase 6 rollout in September 2025. The Customs Decisions System was given its legal framework by Government Decision No. 222/2026 and was fully operational by June 2026, with all 17 types of applications and authorisations handled electronically. In October 2025 the Government approved a programme for harmonising customs information systems for 2025-2030. Beyond adoption, there is shown effect: the Commission reports that the transit system made possible Moldova's full accession to the Common Transit Convention in November 2025 and significantly enhanced the interoperability of its customs operations, and the evidence attributes this result firmly to the transit system. The Commission also judged the related Reform Agenda steps satisfactorily fulfilled. Only three of the programme's 25 systems are operational, implementation of the Union Customs Code remains incomplete because of transitional provisions and a lack of IT tools, and the Government states that the programme has no budget coverage. What remains is the Customs Code amendments and most of the programme's systems, including the core interconnectivity systems and a single window. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is High and tractability is High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-036 · Moldova

National e-services portal limited in range and use

Technology and AI Digital government and digital public services

The national e-services portal offers too few transactional services, is little used, or does not serve all users.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
▲Tractability High Validated

The EU expects Moldova to offer a full range of public services online through its national portal, used by all groups. The Reform Agenda set two conditions: an e-government ecosystem for business services by December 2025, and the EVO Sign digital wallet integrating at least 20 digital public services by December 2026. Moldova launched the EVO application in June 2024 and EVO 2.0 in June 2026, brought services together on the integrated EVO portal, and set up 118 Unified Public Service Centres to give rural residents access to electronic services. The Commission reports that 447 of the 636 services on the EVO portal, 70.3 percent, are available online, and that by June 2026 82 percent of business services and 61 percent of citizen services were digitalised. It verified that 310 of 414 business services are digitalised, meeting the 75 percent objective, although only 133 run fully end to end. User uptake increased significantly, including in rural areas, but the Commission gives no rural figure and low demand persists there. The portal lacks integration with EU systems, and its link to the Single Digital Gateway is still planned. What remains is a fuller range of citizen services delivered end to end online, integration with EU systems, and use by people with weaker digital access or skills. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is High and tractability is High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    20 EU requirement items, 2023 to 2026.

    The 2022 Opinion recorded only that the Government's Action Plan for 2021-2022 set objectives on extending electronic services for citizens and entrepreneurs. In 2023 the Commission found digitalisation lagging behind, with about 40 percent of government services for businesses available online, and set this against the weak results of the Digital Moldova 2020 strategy, which reached 12 percent of services online against a 100 percent objective. In 2024 it noted notable progress on digitalising public services but still put about 40 percent of mapped services online, with varying delivery conditions. The 2025 Reform Agenda turned the requirement into dated payment conditions and noted the portal's lack of integration with EU systems, and the 2025 report found over half of mapped services available digitally. By 2026 the Commission's language had moved from availability to uptake: it reported a significant increase in use while noting persistent low demand in rural areas. The Commission's measures differ from report to report, so the percentages are not strictly comparable. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated

    The Reform Agenda target of 75% of business services digitalised has been met, and EVO, the public services portal and 118 Unified Public Service Centres are in use; but in 2026 only 61% of citizen services are digitalised, only 133 of 414 business services run fully end to end, the Reform Agenda notes that the portal lacks integration with EU systems, and the link to the Single Digital Gateway is still planned. Demand remains low in rural areas, which is why the Commission says the centres were set up. What remains is a fuller range of citizen services delivered end to end online, integration with EU systems, and use by people with weaker digital access or skills.

    ↑Direction of travel Improving Validated

    The Chapter 10 scale is context only, though its progress wording cites the digitalisation of public services in 2024 and progress on all key performance indicators in 2025. Commission figures are about 40% in both 2023 (business services online) and 2024 (mapped services) and rise from then on, on differing measures: over 50% in 2025 (64% for businesses and 54% for individuals in 2024), and in 2026 70.3% of the 636 services on the EVO portal online, 82% of business and 61% of citizen services digitalised and user uptake up significantly. Government counts of 2023 business service requests conflict between its 2024 and 2025 documents, so they are not used for the trend.

  6. Comparator evidence Stated
    CMP-0015

    North Macedonia

    What was done: North Macedonia's national e-services portal, in use since December 2019, reached 338 services by the end of August 2026, including partly available ones, and the Commission reports that its usage rate doubled from the previous year, after the most-demanded certificates went online in 2025. The rise starts from a low level of use, the rate is not defined, and the Commission links it to the new services only by saying that the two went together.

    Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: in North Macedonia, use of the portal rose in the year the services citizens most often request went online, after years in which a growing count of rarely requested services left use low. Moldova's remaining gap sits in a similar place: 61% of citizen services are digitalised against 82% for businesses, and rural demand, which the Commission found low in 2025, rose significantly in 2026, including in rural areas where 118 service centres were set up to respond to persistently low demand. The case suggests ranking further digitalisation by how often citizens request a service, and testing the audit's stated causes of low use, promotion and the price of electronic against paper documents; Moldova's own strategy already proposes lower fees for digital services.

    ▲Comparator relevance High Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

  7. Lesson Assessed

    Three points recur. First, which services go online may matter more than how many. In North Macedonia use stayed low while a growing count of rarely requested services went online, and rose in the year that birth, marriage and citizenship certificates were added. Moldova's remaining gap sits among citizen services, of which 61% were digitalised by June 2026 against 82% of business services. Second, a count of services delivered does not show that they work end to end or are used. Montenegro developed 57 e-services in 2025 with Reform Agenda support, yet the Commission says their operability still needs to be improved. Moldova's own figures show the same gap: of 414 business services, 310 are counted as digitalised but 133 run fully end to end. Third, consolidation on one portal does not by itself close a digital divide or pay for upkeep. Albania offers 95% of applications for 1,257 services online, yet in 2026 the Commission asks it to address an emerging digital divide, resolve accessibility problems and plan and budget for maintaining its platforms. Moldova has decided, in a government decision known from machine translation, to strengthen access to e-services through EVO, and its Government says the cost of digitalisation exceeds its own resources. Agent synthesis, validated at G6b

  8. Priority Assessed

    ▲Priority High Validated

    Digital public services are the subject of two Reform Agenda payment conditions: the EVO Sign wallet integrating at least 20 e-services by December 2026, which is still open and shared with the electronic identification issue, and 75% of business services digitalised, which the Commission found met in 2026. The Commission's 2024 Chapter 10 progress wording cites notable progress on digitalising public services, and the portal and its services are central to the digital government theme, so the rating rests on the open wallet condition rather than on the fulfilled step.

    ▲Tractability High Validated

    Progress has been steady and measured by the Commission in every report from 2023 to 2026, the e-Governance Agency runs the shared platforms, and the work is tied to Reform Agenda funding. The main constraints are cost, which the Government says exceeds its own resources, and low demand among older and rural users.

  9. Policy option Assessed
    RI-TEC-036Internal draft Agent synthesis

    Option 1: Rank the remaining citizen services by how often people request them, put them online end to end in that order, and follow use after each addition

    Details
    Comparator it draws on
    North Macedonia
    Gap it addresses
    the fuller range of citizen services delivered end to end, with 61% of citizen services digitalised, and low demand among some users.
    Rationale
    North Macedonia (relevance High), where the usage rate doubled as the most-demanded certificates went online.
    Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
    Conditional: the rate has no stated definition, it rose alongside Single Sign-On integration, and North Macedonia's range is narrower than Moldova's, so each added service may matter less in Moldova.
    Problem it targets
    low uptake of systems already in place (MEC-11).
    Preconditions
    data on how often each service is requested, on every channel, and a measure of use per service. Moldova's current measures, such as the share of public service users who accessed services electronically and active users of the EVO application, are defined differently and would need to be followed over time; both figures come from machine-translated government documents.
    Risks
    the most-requested services may depend on registers and data exchange that are not ready; added services may not reach older and rural users, since people aged 18 to 29 use e-services three times as often as those aged 60 to 74, according to a machine-translated government programme.
    Responsible actor
    the e-Governance Agency, which runs the shared platforms, with the institutions that own the services.
    RI-TEC-036Internal draft Agent synthesis

    Option 2: Test whether lower fees for digital services and promotion of the portal raise use

    Details
    Comparator it draws on
    North Macedonia
    Gap it addresses
    use of the portal by people who still apply in person, and the persistent low demand the Commission records.
    Rationale
    North Macedonia's State Audit Office tied earlier low use to weak promotion and equal prices for electronic and paper documents, in a finding known from machine translation. Moldova's own strategy already proposes lower fees or shorter delivery times for digital services.
    Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
    Conditional: the account of causes rests on one machine-translated audit, and no case shows the effect of a price change.
    Problem it targets
    low uptake (MEC-11).
    Preconditions
    a test designed so that its effect on use can be measured, for example on a few high-volume services.
    Risks
    lost fee income for a Government that says digitalisation already costs more than its resources; lower fees that do not reach people without digital access or skills.
    Responsible actor
    the Government, with the institutions that set fees for their services.
    RI-TEC-036Internal draft Agent synthesis

RI-TEC-037 · Moldova

Sector and local online public services limited

Technology and AI Digital government and digital public services

Online public services run by sector bodies or municipalities, outside the national portal, are limited in range, use or quality.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▲Priority High Validated
▲Tractability High Validated

The Commission has asked Moldova in four successive reports to digitalise processes for businesses: to simplify and digitalise processes to cut administrative burden in 2023 and 2024, and to digitalise the processes of the Entrepreneurship Development Organisation in 2025 and 2026. The Reform Agenda required an e-government ecosystem for business services, a fully operational State Register of Legal Units and a life events methodology by December 2025. The register portal was launched on 29 December 2025 and the methodology approved on 18 December 2025, and the Commission verified that 310 of 414 business services are digitalised, meeting the 75% objective, and judged the step satisfactorily fulfilled. That outcome is assessed as having worked, but only 133 of the 414 services are fully digital end to end. By June 2026, 82% of business services and 61% of citizen services were digitalised, and the Commission reports that use of e-services increased significantly, including in rural areas, though it gives no rural figure and does not attribute the rise to the public service centres set up there. An audit of the permits system found improved accessibility but only partial use and some reluctance by authorities, a mixed result. The systems of the entrepreneurship and employment agencies are still being procured or built. What remains is end-to-end online delivery and wider use of sector services, especially for citizens and in agencies such as the entrepreneurship and employment agencies. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is High and tractability is High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    20 EU requirement items, 2023 to 2026.

    The 2022 Opinion contains no item on the issue in the evidence. The 2023 and 2024 key recommendations framed it as reducing administrative burden by simplifying and digitalising processes. Alongside, the Commission's measures of availability rose from about 40% of mapped services available digitally in 2024 to over 50% in 2025, with 64% for businesses and 54% for individuals in 2024, while noting each time that delivery conditions vary. In 2025 the Commission also flagged low demand, especially in rural areas, and narrowed the key recommendation to the entrepreneurship agency's processes, which it repeats in 2026. The Reform Agenda business services step was met in March 2026, and the 2026 report records 82% of business and 61% of citizen services digitalised. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated

    The business services reform is in place, with the State Register of Legal Units launched in December 2025 and the life events methodology approved, and the Commission judges the payment step satisfactorily fulfilled. Still, only 133 of the 414 business services counted are fully digital end to end, citizen services lag at 61%, the Commission noted low demand in 2025, and the systems of the entrepreneurship agency and the employment agency are still being procured or built. What remains is end-to-end online delivery and wider use of sector services, especially for citizens and in agencies such as the entrepreneurship and employment agencies.

    ↑Direction of travel Improving Validated

    The chapter scale was used as context only, since this is part of the chapter. The Commission finds about 40% of mapped services available digitally in 2024, over 50% in 2025 with 64% for businesses and 54% for individuals in 2024, and 82% of business services and 61% of citizen services by June 2026, and its 2026 release decision confirms that the Reform Agenda objective of 75% of business services was met. The 2026 report also finds that user uptake increased significantly, including in rural areas.

    ▲Priority High Validated

    Digital services for businesses are the subject of key recommendations in four reports: digitalising processes to cut administrative burden in 2023 and 2024, and digitalising the entrepreneurship agency's processes in 2025 and 2026. The related Reform Agenda payment step (75% of business services digitalised, with the State Register of Legal Units and the life events methodology) is met, so the rating rests on the repeated recommendations; online public services are central to the digital government theme.

    ▲Tractability High Validated

    There is strong evidence of past progress, with the share of business services online rising each year from 2024 to 2026 and the payment step met. The work is led by the e-Governance Agency and the State Chancellery with shared platforms, although sector agencies and rural demand still need attention.

RI-FMW-011 · Moldova

Access to healthcare for EU citizens through the European Health Insurance Card

Chapter 2

EU citizens can use the European Health Insurance Card or access medical services only where a bilateral arrangement exists, so access is not yet available to citizens of all Member States.

∅Direction of travel Insufficient evidence Validated
■Unresolved gap Open Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The European Health Insurance Card is part of the Chapter 2 acquis on social security coordination, and the Commission's 2025 and 2026 key recommendations ask Moldova to develop the IT infrastructure and capacity for the Card scheme alongside the Electronic Exchange of Social Security Information. The Government stated in 2025, in machine-translated documents, that the EU acts on the Card are not transposed in Moldova, that Moldova is to apply the Card, and that it plans a law on cross-border medical care in EU Member States, the European Economic Area and Switzerland by December 2026. The Commission reports that Moldova conducted a feasibility study on introducing the Card, finalised in August 2026, and that an action plan on the Card was approved the same month as a roadmap for operational implementation. No source shows the law adopted or the Card issued, and no item states whether EU citizens can obtain healthcare in Moldova with the Card, so no outcome has been assessed. The international cooperation section of the health insurance fund that deals with Member State institutions has three specialists. What remains is a decision on introducing the Card and the legal and financial arrangements that would give EU citizens access to healthcare through it. The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel is insufficient evidence. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    No EU requirement item recorded.

    No requirement item on the Card from the 2022 Opinion or the 2023 and 2024 reports was found. The Card first appears in the 2025 report, whose key recommendation names IT infrastructure and capacity for the Card scheme to be developed together with the Electronic Exchange of Social Security Information, and whose sub-area wording records no progress on the Card. The 2026 report repeats the key recommendation and records the feasibility study and the action plan, so the Commission's attention moves from the absence of progress to the first preparatory steps. Both reports address the domestic preconditions for the Card rather than whether EU citizens can use it in Moldova. No Reform Agenda payment condition on the Card was found in the evidence. RI-TEC-001 · Moldova

Artificial intelligence framework not aligned or supported by structures

Technology and AI Artificial intelligence

The rules on artificial intelligence are not aligned with the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, or the enforcement structures and wider capacity needed to apply them and support trustworthy uptake are not in place.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
■Unresolved gap Open Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to develop the governance, regulatory and enforcement structures needed for artificial intelligence in line with the EU AI Act. Moldova has published a White Paper on data governance and AI, which the Government itself describes as declarative and not a policy document as such, and in 2024 it set up a sub-council on AI and data governance within the National Digitalisation Council. A law on AI, a law on AI testing spaces, a 2026 to 2030 national programme and an AI governance institution are all planned or being drafted, with transposition of the AI Act foreseen by the end of 2026 or by 2027. Little is shown to have happened: a civil society report finds that the sub-council produced no initiative for a legal framework on AI in 2024 and 2025 as planned. The Government reported in 2025 that no institution responsible for AI policy or supervision had been identified and that no ministry employee covered AI, and in 2026 it described the field as at an early stage, without a competent authority or an AI-specific legal framework. Funding for the national programme will depend on the annual budget process. What remains is a law aligned with the AI Act, a designated and staffed supervisory authority, and the governance structure to apply it. Most Government sources are machine translated. The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

Not ready for EU justice, home affairs and border information systems

Technology and AI Interoperability and electronic systems Data and data governance

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
■Unresolved gap Open Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The EU asks Moldova to prepare its justice, home affairs and border information systems for connection to EU large-scale systems. In 2026 the Commission found that the migration inspectorate's systems need upgrading for interoperability with national and EU IT systems, and that the border police system's security and data protection weaknesses must be addressed in anticipation of a future connection to EU large-scale IT systems; it also asks for better data exchange through Europol's SIENA channel. Moldova has rolled out SIENA to several law enforcement bodies, and the Commission states that exchanges through it have increased, although it gives no figures. For the EU systems themselves, the responses are plans: interoperability of the fingerprint register with Eurodac by June 2028, a national visa system interoperable with the EU Visa Information System, an analysis by the end of 2027 of how to connect the criminal records register to ECRIS and ECRIS-TCN, and a joint study with eu-LISA. The Government reports that amendments to the fingerprint law partially transpose the Eurodac Regulation, a step in law only. What remains is building or upgrading the migration, border and justice systems so that they are secure and ready to connect to Eurodac, the Visa Information System, ECRIS and the other EU large-scale systems. The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-039 · Moldova

Public sector websites and apps not accessible to persons with disabilities

Technology and AI Digital government and digital public services

Public sector websites, mobile applications and other digital public services are not accessible to persons with physical, sensory or intellectual disabilities, and the EU accessibility requirements for them (the Web Accessibility Directive and the European Accessibility Act) are not applied or enforced.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
■Unresolved gap Open Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to improve the accessibility of public sector websites, mobile applications and audiovisual services for persons with physical, sensory and intellectual disabilities. Moldova has guidelines for government websites, and its digital strategy implementation programme includes an action to make ICT products and services accessible, including rules based on the WCAG 2.2 guidelines. That action had not started by April 2026, because the e-Governance Agency order setting the WCAG 2.2 rules awaits a prior Government Decision on accessibility requirements. In August 2026 Moldova adopted a law on accessibility requirements for certain products and services, including digital and e-commerce services, which the Commission describes as in line with the acquis. This is an adopted law, not a shown result, and it concerns products and services rather than public sector websites. No improvement in practice is shown. In 2023 SIGMA found poor compliance with the WCAG 2.0 standard, with an average of 45 errors per page and only one of 26 sampled government websites faring well. In 2026 the Commission found public sector websites and mobile applications still insufficiently accessible, and accessibility insufficiently enforced and funded. What remains is binding accessibility rules for public sector websites and applications, with enforcement and funding. The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    4 EU requirement items, 2026.

    The requirement is new as an EU ask. The Commission did not raise the accessibility of public sector websites and applications in any report in the evidence before 2026, although SIGMA, an international partner, had documented poor compliance in 2023. The 2026 report raised it at once as a key recommendation, asking Moldova to improve the accessibility of public sector websites, mobile applications and audiovisual services. In the same report the Commission found that public sector websites and mobile applications remain insufficiently accessible, that accessibility is insufficiently enforced and funded across buildings, transport, websites and digital services, and that public and private job portals are largely inaccessible. It also welcomed the August 2026 law on accessibility requirements for products and services. No Reform Agenda payment condition names the issue, so there is no sequence of Commission wording to compare. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-040 · Moldova

Semiconductor acquis not aligned

Technology and AI Digitalisation of government or economic activity

Legislation is not aligned with the EU acquis on semiconductors, in particular the Chips Act.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
■Unresolved gap Open Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
▽Tractability Low Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to align its legislation with the EU acquis on semiconductors, in particular the Chips Act. In April 2026 Moldova adopted a law on the protection of topographies of semiconductor products, but this is an intellectual property measure rather than alignment with the Chips Act, which the Commission says Moldova is yet to achieve. The Government plans to transpose the Chips Act by the end of 2026 and lists a draft law on investments for the purpose, but neither has been reported as adopted. The Government states that there are no national rules on planning, building or operating semiconductor production facilities and no public authority designated to examine such applications, that no institution is responsible for the area and that no ministry employee covers it. The economy ministry is to take on the policy area and a new principal consultant post is planned. The Government describes the sector in Moldova as at an early stage and almost non-existent. What remains is transposition of the Chips Act and the designation and staffing of a competent authority. The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is Medium and tractability is Low. Agent synthesis, validated at G7
