RI-FMW-001 · Moldova

Nationality discrimination in access to employment

Chapter 2

The law governing access to the labour market does not give EU workers equal treatment with nationals, for example by treating them as any other foreigner or reserving private sector posts for nationals.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
▲Tractability High Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to align its legislation with the EU acquis on access for EU citizens to the labour market and, from 2026, on equal treatment of EU workers. Amendments to the law on the regime of foreigners in force since January 2024 let EU citizens work in Moldova without a work permit, and Law No. 200/2025 on the free movement and residence of EU citizens, adopted in July 2025, entered into force in March 2026. The Government states, in machine-translated documents, that the law gives EU citizens and their family members equal treatment with Moldovan citizens. No source yet describes how the law is applied, and no outcome has been assessed. The secondary and sectoral legislation needed to give EU workers equal access to employment services, active measures, service housing and private placement is still at draft or planning stage, and private employment agencies could until now be licensed only if their staff held Moldovan citizenship. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is improving, legal only. Priority is Medium and tractability is High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    4 EU requirement items, 2023 to 2026.

    No requirement item from the 2022 Opinion is held for this issue. In February 2023 the Commission's analytical report found that the legal framework on access to the labour market did not differentiate between EU workers and other third-country nationals, and that family members of EU workers followed the same rules as those of other foreign workers. Access for EU citizens was not among the key recommendations of the 2023 and 2024 reports, although the 2023 report contained a general call to align legislation with the acquis. The 2025 report made it a key recommendation to align national legislation with the acquis on access for EU citizens to the labour market. In 2026, after Law No. 200/2025 entered into force, the wording became "continue alignment" and was widened to include equal treatment of EU workers. Over the same years the Commission's rating of the whole chapter moved from early stage in 2023 and 2024 to some level of preparation in 2025 and between some and moderate in 2026. No benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on the issue was found. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

By accession, EU workers and their family members must no longer face work permits or similar conditions, yet in 2023 the Commission found that EU citizens needed an employer-requested temporary residence permit for work and numerous documents, and that their family members were treated as other foreign workers. Moldova amended the law on the regime of foreigners, and from January 2024 EU citizens could work without a work permit. In July 2025 it adopted Law No. 200/2025, under which EU citizens need no work authorisation and, for stays over 90 days, a residence card not tied to a purpose of stay; the Commission reports that the law entered into force in March 2026. These are adopted laws, not shown results. Practice lags: after the General Inspectorate for Migration approved an operating procedure in March 2026, 28 applications for the new residence documents had been submitted, while 422 EU citizens were still to be documented under the old stay-for-work regime in 2025. Full separation of the two regimes depends on a draft law on foreigners that would enter into force on 1 June 2027, and the Ministry of Internal Affairs still needs to revise its rules on registering EU citizens. Most Government sources are machine translated. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is improving, mainly in law. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. RI-FMW-003 · Moldova

Public sector posts closed to EU citizens beyond the public authority exception

Chapter 2

EU citizens are barred from public sector posts other than a short list of exemptions, rather than only from posts involving the exercise of public authority and safeguarding the general interests of the State.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The issue is whether EU citizens are barred from public sector posts beyond those that involve the exercise of public authority and the safeguarding of the general interests of the State, which are the only posts that may be reserved for nationals. From 2023 to 2025 the Commission found that EU citizens had no access to posts in public administration bodies. Government Decision No. 566/2025 allows technical, specialist and auxiliary posts to be filled by persons without Moldovan citizenship under employment contracts. The Commission's 2026 report confirms that the new legislation opened these posts to EU citizens, while civil servant posts remain restricted to Moldovan nationals. No source reports EU citizens actually recruited to the opened posts, so the change is shown in law, not in practice. The Government's own account still excludes public functions that expressly require Moldovan citizenship, and it plans an analysis, including the case law of the Court of Justice, before deciding which further functions or posts can be opened. What remains is opening civil servant posts to EU citizens, except those involving the exercise of public authority. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is improving, legal only. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-FMW-005 · Moldova

Employment service capacity for EURES and labour mobility

Chapter 2

The public employment service lacks trained staff or adequate IT and data systems to take part in EU labour mobility networks and vacancy exchange.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to ensure the capacity, resources and IT infrastructure, systems and databases needed for full participation in EURES, the Electronic Exchange of Social Security Information system and the EHIC scheme. Moldova has set up a Labour Migration and EURES department in the National Employment Agency from January 2025, with five of its six posts filled, assigned the Agency the role of EURES National Coordination Office, and developed technical standards, procedures and formats for matching vacancies and CVs with the EURES portal. The Commission reports that the Agency developed a new integrated information system in December 2025, aiming at fully digitalised services by 2027, and a 2026 Government document says the system, funded by the EU Delegation, is still being developed. No source shows the new system in use, and the Agency's own reports for 2025 and 2026 state that the lack of a modern information system affects the efficiency and quality of its services. Interoperability with the EURES platform, staff training on EURES and minimum requirements for personal data in that exchange are planned for 2028 and are not reported as delivered. What remains is a working connection between the Agency's information system and the EURES platform, operated by trained staff, before accession. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

National social security law not aligned with the coordination regulations

Chapter 2

National pension, health and other social security laws are only partly aligned with the EU coordination regulations, for example through citizenship conditions, and the administrative measures for applying them at accession are not identified or in place.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The EU requires Moldova's national social security law to be aligned with the coordination regulations, Regulations (EC) No 883/2004 and No 987/2009, and in 2026 the Commission asked Moldova to provide gap analyses for those regulations. In 2023 the Commission found that national law covered most branches of social security but not pre-retirement benefits, and that non-nationals with temporary residence received no unemployment benefit. Moldova has since adopted a law setting the legal basis for applying the EU coordination rules and connecting to the Electronic Exchange of Social Security Information. A draft law on unemployment benefit would create the framework to apply Articles 64 and 65 of Regulation 883/2004 and introduce the notion of frontier worker, but its section on EU mobility would apply only from accession. No source describes the adopted law being applied, and the Government states that current law does not regulate keeping unemployment benefit when moving to another Member State or registering EU jobseekers in Moldova. Specialist capacity is thin: the health insurance fund's legal directorate has 3 of 8 planned staff working on harmonisation. What remains is a gap analysis and full alignment of pension, health, unemployment and other social security law, with the administrative measures to apply it at accession. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is improving, legal only. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

    ↑Direction of travel Improving Validated

    The 2023 analytical report found that national law covers most branches of social security but not pre-retirement benefits, gives no unemployment benefit to non-nationals with temporary residence, and needs capacity building in coordination; a search of all 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files found no Commission item on this alignment in the 2024 or 2025 reports, so the wording is not repeated across three reports and the default of persistent does not apply. The 2026 report records the adoption of a law setting a legal basis for applying the coordination rules, which is improvement in law only: the Commission does not assess its alignment and asks for gap analyses of the coordination regulations, and the 2023 gap on unemployment benefit remains open. The Chapter 2 rating rose from an early stage in 2023 and 2024 to between some and a moderate level of preparation in 2026, but the progress it cites concerns bilateral agreements and EURES, so the scale was not decisive.

RI-FMW-010 · Moldova

Readiness for electronic exchange of social security information

Chapter 2

The institutions lack the IT and human capacity to exchange social security information electronically with Member States (the EESSI system) and to use electronic health insurance data.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to develop the IT infrastructure, systems, databases and administrative and financial capacity needed for full participation in the Electronic Exchange of Social Security Information (EESSI) system and the EHIC scheme. In February 2026 Moldova designated the e-Governance Agency as the EESSI National Access Point and the National Office of Social Insurance and the National Health Insurance Company as liaison bodies, adopted a law setting the legal basis for EU social security coordination rules and EESSI interconnection, and approved an EESSI Action Plan. These steps are adopted, but no source reports the access point or liaison bodies working or any data exchanged, and Moldova is not connected to EESSI. The Government reports that the information systems of the employment agency and the social insurance house still need to be adjusted for EESSI, that the technical solution and its financing will be chosen only after technical documentation arrives from the Commission, and that 3 of 8 planned IT staff at the health insurance company work on the EHIC and interconnection with European systems. What remains is the IT infrastructure, interconnected systems, staff and funding for full participation in EESSI and for electronic exchange of health insurance data. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is improving, organisationally and legally only, as no technical connection is reported. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-004 · Moldova

Core e-government building blocks missing

Technology and AI Digital government and digital public services Digitalisation of government or economic activity Interoperability and electronic systems

Shared systems that every institution needs to work digitally, such as a single document management system, legal and technical arrangements for electronic archiving, a digital mailbox and shared administrative information systems, are missing or little used.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated Flagged for re-review
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The EU's requirement under this issue centres on the civil service human resources information system: the Commission found national HR systems non-functional, and the Reform Agenda requires a human resource management information system for all central government institutions, with at least three modules operational, by December 2027. Moldova has a long-standing set of shared e-government platforms, including MCloud, MPass, MPay and MConnect, which the Reform Agenda records as already implemented, and a World Bank-supported project added platforms such as MDelivery, MPower and MDocs. Some of these are shown in use: the Commission reported 42 more services integrated with MDelivery in 2023, and the permits system had issued permits through 16 of the 31 issuing institutions when audited. The HR system has not followed: the earlier system failed through problems with its private provider, and its replacement was in incipient design in 2025 and still in development in 2026. Institutions not subordinate to the Government declined to use the permits system, and the eArhiva electronic archive is still a planned action. Sources disagree on whether all state information systems are registered in the state register. What remains is a working HR management system and consistent use of shared systems by all institutions. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-005 · Moldova

Limited taxpayer e-services

Technology and AI Digital government and digital public services

The tax administration offers a limited range of electronic services to taxpayers.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
▲Tractability High Validated

The Commission's 2026 report states that it is essential for Moldova to further increase the digitalisation of tax services, and the Reform Agenda sets a target of 18 of 19 taxpayer services, or 90%, digitalised for businesses and citizens by December 2026. The digitalisation of State Tax Service services is planned, with at least two services to be digitalised by 2025 and two more in 2026, but no source reports which services have so far been digitalised, so the measure remains proposed. The e-Invoice service on the Electronic Fiscal Services platform is in place and is assessed as implemented. On use, the Government's own machine-translated indicator gives 64% of companies using electronic invoices against a target above 70%, a figure not independently corroborated, and SIGMA found that for fiscal year 2022 81% of businesses declared corporate income tax digitally but only 10% of citizens filed personal income tax returns electronically. These figures describe uptake, not whether the services meet the EU requirement. The Reform Agenda names limited staff and time, and many taxpayers' preference for in-person service, as barriers. What remains is completing the digitalisation of taxpayer services and raising their use, especially by citizens. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is Medium and tractability is High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

    7 EU requirement items, 2023 to 2026.

From 2023 the Commission's wording is a finding of improvement rather than a demand: the 2023 report states that the tax administration improved its services to taxpayers, including electronic tax returns, and the 2024 report that it improved its electronic services and promoted voluntary compliance. The 2025 report and the 2026 report record good progress in Chapter 16 that includes the digitalisation of tax administration services, though these statements cover the whole chapter. The Reform Agenda turned the matter into a payment condition with a numerical target for December 2026. The 2026 report then returns to a requirement, stating that further digitalisation of tax services is essential alongside an automated compliance risk management system. No key recommendation names taxpayer e-services. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-011 · Moldova

Electronic communications law not aligned with EU rules

Technology and AI Digital infrastructure and connectivity

The law on electronic communications is not fully aligned with the European Electronic Communications Code, the Gigabit Infrastructure Act and related rules on cost reduction, spectrum, roaming and open internet access.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
▲Tractability High Validated

The Commission asked Moldova to align its law with the European Electronic Communications Code and the EU roaming acquis, including their secondary legislation, so that it could join the Roam Like at Home area. Parliament adopted Electronic Communications Law No. 72/2025 in April 2025 and roaming Law No. 81/2025 in the same month, the regulator adopted detailed roaming rules, and Law No. 106 of June 2026 transposes the Gigabit Infrastructure Act. Law No. 72/2025 entered into force on 1 January 2026. The Commission assessed the legislation as correctly transposing the whole EU roaming acquis and judged the related Reform Agenda step satisfactorily fulfilled. On that basis Moldova joined Roam Like at Home on 1 January 2026, and the Commission states that this removed roaming charges and brought immediate benefits to citizens and businesses; the roaming outcome is assessed as having worked. Earlier, the voluntary operator agreement of 2023 led to reduced roaming tariffs from January 2024, which the Commission and an independent civil society source both report. For the Code itself, effects on network roll-out are too early to judge, as the law has applied only since January 2026. The regulator is still drafting secondary acts under the new law and plans an end-user protection regulation for 2026, the Government plans to transpose the remaining electronic communications acts by the end of 2027, and a civil society monitor finds the law only partially compatible with the Code. What remains is completing and applying the secondary legislation under the Code and the Gigabit Infrastructure Act and transposing the remaining related acts. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is Medium and tractability is High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    15 EU requirement items, 2022 to 2026.

    The 2022 Opinion found Moldova's alignment with the EU electronic communications framework limited. The 2023 report asked for alignment with the Electronic Communications Code and for alignment with and implementation of the Roaming Regulation. In 2024 the key recommendation linked alignment with the roaming acquis and the Code to joining the Roam Like at Home area, and the report found that alignment had started. The 2025 report narrowed the request to implementing secondary legislation and noted legislative advances on roaming. The Reform Agenda step on electronic communications was then found satisfactorily fulfilled. The 2026 report records the Code transposed in primary law, secondary legislation approximated and the Gigabit Infrastructure Act reflected in the June 2026 law, and it contains no recommendation on electronic communications or roaming. RI-TEC-012 · Moldova

Electronic communications regulator independence and market oversight weak

Technology and AI Digital infrastructure and connectivity

The electronic communications regulator lacks guaranteed independence in appointments and funding and sufficient capacity, and competitive safeguards in a concentrated telecom market are not applied.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
▲Tractability High Validated

The issue concerns the independence and capacity of the electronic communications regulator and competitive safeguards in a concentrated telecom market, where Moldtelecom, the national operator, holds more than half of the broadband market. The Reform Agenda sets a step for June 2026 under which at least 3% of the incumbent's infrastructure is shared, and commits the incumbent to network-sharing agreements in line with the Gigabit Infrastructure Act. Moldova adopted Electronic Communications Law No. 72/2025, in force from 1 January 2026, under which the regulator was renamed ARCOM, and the Commission finds that the new legal framework reinforced its administrative and financial independence. Updated infrastructure access tariffs, between 16% and 49% lower, entered into force on 1 March 2026, and Law No. 106 of 11 June 2026 transposed the Gigabit Infrastructure Act. The regulator had 105 staff for 114 posts in March 2026 and signed working arrangements with BEREC in March 2025. No source reports how the independence provisions are applied, the network-sharing agreements are still only a commitment, and no item reports the sharing rate after the 0.95% baseline. The one outcome assessed, from the BEREC arrangements, rests only on the regulator's own report, so its success is insufficient evidence. What remains is independence shown in practice and safeguards that actually raise infrastructure sharing. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is improving, legal only for independence. Priority is Medium and tractability is High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    No EU requirement item recorded.

    No item from the 2022 Opinion, and no benchmark or key recommendation, addresses the regulator's independence; the Commission mentions it only in its 2026 finding that the new law reinforced it. Against that, the Government's 2025 programme reports, in machine translation, an ITU finding that the regulator's independence and accountability are insufficient. The competition side was given concrete terms by the Reform Agenda in 2025, which found network sharing with the incumbent minimal at 0.95% of infrastructure, driving up deployment costs and discouraging new entrants, and set the target of at least 3% shared by June 2026 through implementation of the Electronic Communications Code. By 2026 the Commission was recording delivery against these conditions: lower access tariffs and the transposing law on access to property and infrastructure. The Commission's rating of the whole of Chapter 10 moved from some level of preparation in 2023, 2024 and 2025 to moderately prepared in 2026, which covers more than this issue. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated

    The Reform Agenda requires at least 3% of the incumbent's infrastructure to be shared and network-sharing agreements by the incumbent; access tariffs have been cut and the Gigabit Infrastructure Act transposed in June 2026, but the agreements are still planned and no item among the 3,631 items held in the Moldova evidence files reports the sharing rate after the 0.95% baseline. The law reinforcing the regulator's independence is adopted, and the regulator had filled 105 of 114 posts by March 2026. What remains is independence shown in practice and competitive safeguards that actually raise infrastructure sharing in a market where the incumbent holds more than half of broadband.

    ↑Direction of travel Improving Validated

    The Chapter 10 scale is context only, since this is part of the chapter: some level of preparation from 2023 to 2025 and moderately prepared in 2026. The 2026 report finds that the new legal framework reinforced the regulator's administrative and financial independence, and the Commission's 2026 release decision records access tariffs for the incumbent's infrastructure cut by 16% to 49% from 1 March 2026, against minimal network sharing (0.95%) in the 2025 baseline. The gain on independence is legal only, and an ITU finding reported in the Government's 2025 programme still describes independence and accountability as insufficient (machine translated).

RI-TEC-013 · Moldova

Broadband and high-capacity network coverage uneven

Technology and AI Digital infrastructure and connectivity

Small businesses and rural or non-urban areas face obstacles to fixed broadband, and high-capacity and 5G networks are still being rolled out.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission has asked Moldova to prioritise infrastructure investment to overcome the rural-urban digital divide, and it reports that 5G coverage remains well below the EU average. Moldova's regulator set licence conditions for the 700 MHz and 800 MHz bands in August 2024, with coverage obligations from October 2027, and awarded spectrum to three operators in February 2025 and to Moldtelecom in a further 2025 competition. A new law on electronic communications entered into force in January 2026, and it requires the regulator to survey broadband coverage. Coverage and take-up are shown to have risen: home internet access went from 67.5% of households in 2023 to nearly 95% in 2026, fixed-broadband connections rose by 6.9% in the year to early 2026, and median download speeds rose by about a third. The Commission estimates 5G population coverage at 25 to 35%, and the success of the spectrum awards is assessed as too early to judge. What remains is high-capacity fixed and 5G coverage in rural and small localities: the Government counts 431 localities without fixed broadband, most of them small and isolated, and the plan to build networks there waits for the regulator's survey. Much of the Government and regulator evidence is machine translated. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    8 EU requirement items, 2023 to 2026.

    The Commission's concern has narrowed from a general one to a specific one. In 2023 it found that digitalisation in Moldova was lagging behind and that connectivity gaps remained, contrasting near-universal 4G coverage with home internet access of 67.5% of households, and 58% in rural areas. In 2024 an economic key recommendation asked Moldova to prioritise infrastructure investment, including to overcome the rural-urban digital divide. In 2025 the Commission found digitalisation steadily advancing while regional disparities persisted, and the Reform Agenda described a significant urban-rural divide. By 2026 the focus had moved to 5G, with some progress recorded but coverage well below the EU average. No Chapter 10 key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition addresses coverage; the related Reform Agenda step on electronic communications, assessed as satisfactorily fulfilled, concerns legal alignment rather than coverage. RI-TEC-014 · Moldova

Broadband planning and investment framework incomplete

Technology and AI Digital infrastructure and connectivity

National broadband targets, plans and investment are not aligned with EU Digital Decade targets, and EU funding instruments, State aid rules and backhaul studies are not used or in place.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to raise investment in infrastructure, including to overcome the rural-urban digital divide, and the Reform Agenda required a broadband mapping system to support targeted investment. The regulator operates a public broadband coverage platform, expanded since 2025, and Moldova has put into operation a map of very high capacity networks, built on a data-sharing agreement of March 2026 with the cadastre bodies and populated with data from the three mobile operators and the six largest fixed operators. The Commission finds that the two platforms provide relevant monitoring for digital investment decisions. The investment framework itself is less advanced. The regulator's geographical survey of broadband coverage has a legal deadline of 30 December 2030, and network development in white areas is to follow it. Rules on state aid for broadband networks exist only as a planned Competition Council decision. The Government notes that most white-area localities are small and isolated and need significant investment, and the Commission states that infrastructure investment remains significantly below needs. What remains is a national investment framework, with state aid rules and funding, that brings broadband to rural and white areas in line with EU connectivity targets. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    4 EU requirement items, 2023 to 2026.

    The 2023 report asked Moldova to increase investment in infrastructure, especially for energy security, international trade and digitalisation. The 2024 report sharpened this to prioritising investment to overcome the rural-urban digital divide, among other aims. In both years digital infrastructure appears alongside energy and transport rather than as a separate recommendation on broadband. The 2025 Reform Agenda added a specific step, noting that the absence of a comprehensive broadband mapping system restricted monitoring, investment strategies and the targeting of public subsidies, and committing Moldova to develop one. By 2026 the Commission recorded the mapping platforms as providing relevant monitoring, while the 2026 report observed that investment remained significantly below infrastructure needs. RI-TEC-016 · Moldova

Open data and re-use of public sector information incomplete

Technology and AI Data and data governance

Institutions do not regularly publish and update datasets on the open data portal, and legislation is only partly aligned with the Open Data Directive and related EU data rules.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission has found that no authority was responsible for open data policies and that Moldova was not yet aligned with the Open Data Directive, and the 2024 Growth Plan Communication asks Moldova to strengthen implementation of the European data strategy rules, including the Open Data Directive. Parliament adopted Law No. 109/2025 on open data and the reuse of public sector information in May 2025, partially transposing the Directive, followed by methodological rules in Government Decision No. 563/2025, and the ministry created an open data policy service with two staff. The law and rules are adopted, but no source shows their effect on data publication. Civil society states that adoption of the law and continued efforts to implement it have strengthened proactive access to information, but it gives no measure of datasets published or re-used, so success cannot be shown. The only count is the Government's figure of 1,268 datasets on the portal against a target of 1,500 by 2027, and the World Bank found in 2024 that the portal is still lacking in use. The Government itself says the portal needs updating and completing with data, and the draft law on data and data governance has been suspended until 2027. What remains is full alignment with the Open Data Directive and related EU data rules, and regular publication and updating of datasets by institutions. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is improving, legally and institutionally only. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

Weak compliance with data protection rules

Technology and AI Data and data governance Cybersecurity

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated

◆Tractability Medium Validated

The EU asks Moldova to align its data protection legislation further with the acquis, train public servants across all institutions and step up awareness campaigns, and in 2025 it asked Moldova to implement the National Health Strategy with a focus on digitalising health services and protecting personal data. Moldova adopted Law No. 195/2024 to align with the General Data Protection Regulation, in force from 23 August 2026, which lets the data protection authority impose administrative sanctions directly. In 2025 the authority organised 84 courses for over 3,600 people and prepared guidelines on applying the new law, on its own account. Breaches continue: the authority found breaches in 105 of 230 decisions in 2022, 173 violations are reported for 2024 and again for 2025, and in 2025 a breach at the largest private laboratory leaked thousands of patients' test results. Only about 50 public authorities have designated a data protection officer. The Government states that data exchange takes place exclusively through MConnect, while the authority finds that state bodies still access personal data through COI technology, which does not identify individual users. No source yet shows the new law being applied. What remains is compliance in practice by public and private controllers, including in health, with the new sanctions applied and access to state registers made traceable. The unresolved gap is partly_addressed and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-023 · Moldova

Operational cybersecurity capacity of public institutions weak

Technology and AI Cybersecurity

The national incident response centre and state institutions lack staff, expertise and secure infrastructure, so government services and digital infrastructure remain exposed to attacks.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission has asked Moldova to make its new national cybersecurity authority operational, and the Reform Agenda set the step of making the National Agency for Cybersecurity fully operational with a national CERT by December 2025. Moldova established the Agency in December 2023, launched it in February 2024, and brought the law on cybersecurity into force in January 2025. With EU funding, seconded experts and training, the Agency had 32 staff by December 2025, and the Commission reports that it became operational as the single point of contact and national CERT, with an incident management platform in use. The Commission records 38 incidents handled and 52 vulnerability notifications in 2025, and judged the Reform Agenda step satisfactorily fulfilled. Gaps remain in the Agency's own account: supervision was only partly carried out for lack of staff and a complete framework, its security monitoring system was still being configured, its incident playbooks were 70% complete, and it lacks qualified IT specialists. The Government reports that cyber incidents rose by over 30% between 2021 and 2023, and the Commission notes security vulnerabilities in the border police information system. The Agency's reports are machine translated. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    6 EU requirement items, 2023 to 2026.

    The Commission's wording has moved from a missing institution to its operational capacity and then to fulfilment. In 2021 it found that a national CERT foreseen by the 2019 to 2024 information security strategy was pending approval of its mandate. In 2023 it described the Information Technology and Cyber Security Service as the government's incident response team. In 2024, after the Agency was set up, it called for further effort to ensure its operational capacity, and in 2025 it found progress but said further efforts were needed. The Reform Agenda then made the Agency's full operation and a national CERT a step, noting that the Agency lacked staff, IT resources and legal authority. In 2026 the Commission judged the step satisfactorily fulfilled and described the Agency as further strengthened, without repeating a recommendation on its capacity, while pointing to vulnerabilities in a specific state system. RI-TEC-028 · Moldova

Interoperability platform and data exchange underused

Technology and AI Interoperability and electronic systems Data and data governance

Institutions do not use the national interoperability platform regularly, so administrative data are not shared ex officio between institutions, including for checks such as asset declarations and inspections.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to strengthen interoperability between its automated asset verification systems and state registries, and the Reform Agenda requires all declarations to be filed by December 2026 in a new e-Integrity system that is interoperable through the MConnect platform. More broadly, the issue is whether institutions use the national interoperability platform regularly. Moldova has had a law since 2018 requiring agencies to exchange data only through the interoperability solution, with an express duty to connect and sanctions in force since January 2021. SIGMA found MConnect well functioning in 2023, with base registers connected and 336 institutions exchanging data, and the Government reports 144 state and 252 private systems integrated, a different measure. One result is shown: the Commission reports that data exchange through MConnect let the electoral commission check party financing more effectively, though it gives no measure of this. Underuse persists. The World Bank finds that many ministries work in silos, the Government finds its systems fragmented, and the data protection authority reports that 13 entities still access state registers through COI technology outside the platform, with no progress despite repeated requests. In 2026 the Commission found the integrity authority's interoperable verification tools still constrained. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  5. Unresolved gap Assessed

    ◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated

    The platform and the legal duty to exchange data through it are in place, with sanctions since 2021, and SIGMA found the base registers connected to it in 2023. The data protection authority finds that state bodies still access personal data through COI technology outside the platform, which conflicts with the government's statement that data exchange takes place exclusively through MConnect, and the Commission in 2026 still finds the interoperable verification tools for asset declarations not fully functioning. What remains is regular use of the platform by all institutions, including an end to access outside it, and full data exchange for asset declaration checks.

    →Direction of travel Persistent Validated

    The Commission reported in 2023 that data exchange through MConnect let the electoral commission check party financing more effectively, but in 2025 it said interoperability between automated verification systems and state registries must still be strengthened, and in 2026 it noted constraints on the full practical functioning of interoperable verification tools. Other sources show connections continuing (336 institutions in 2023 according to SIGMA; 396 integrated state and private systems in 2025 according to the Government, a different measure) while the same underuse is reported: the World Bank in 2024 found interoperability yet to be streamlined, the government in 2025 found systems fragmented, and the data protection authority in 2026 found state bodies still using COI access outside the platform. The Chapter 10 rating was not decisive, as the issue is cross-cutting.

RI-TEC-034 · Moldova

Digital single market rules not aligned

Technology and AI Digitalisation of government or economic activity

Legislation is not aligned with EU rules on online platforms and services, such as the Digital Services Act, the Digital Markets Act, the platform-to-business and geo-blocking regulations, and e-commerce is developing slowly.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to align with EU digital single market rules on geo-blocking, platform-to-business relations, the Digital Services Act and the Digital Markets Act, and to build the capacity and legal basis to enforce the two Acts from accession. Moldova adopted two laws in 2025 that partly transpose the platform-to-business and geo-blocking regulations, and the Competition Council is designated for the first. Moldova is broadly aligned with the e-Commerce Directive. A digital services law is being drafted with EU4Digital experts, and the Government plans to align with the Digital Services Act and set up mechanisms for the Digital Markets Act by the end of 2026, with new supervisory units in the communications regulator and the Competition Council. These are adopted or planned measures, not shown results. In 2026 the Commission found alignment on geo-blocking and platform-to-business relations still partial and only initial steps on the institutional framework for the two Acts. The Government notes that no authorities yet supervise digital services and markets, that enforcement rules under the platform-to-business regulation are missing, and that one ministry post covers the area. Most Government sources are machine translated. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is improving, legal only. Priority is Medium and tractability is Medium. RI-TEC-035 · Moldova

Digital tools in company law not fully aligned

Technology and AI Digitalisation of government or economic activity

Company law is not fully aligned with EU rules on the use of digital tools and processes, such as online formation, electronic filing and director checks.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
◆Priority Medium Validated
▲Tractability High Validated

The Commission asks Moldova to align its company law with the EU acquis on the use of digital tools and processes, which covers matters such as online company formation and electronic filing. Law No. 175/2021 allowed documents for registering legal entities to be submitted electronically with an electronic signature, and the Commission reported in 2024 that a qualified electronic signature had been introduced for filing documents with the business register. In practice, however, online registration ran by e-mail as a provisional solution because the Public Services Agency's systems were delayed. The new State Register of Legal Entities, planned for July 2025, was launched in December 2025 and enables registration of all legal forms of entities. In February 2026 the platform offered online applications such as name reservation and register extracts, and no source yet shows company formation and filings running fully online at scale. The Government itself considers the EU directive on digital tools in company law only partially transposed, and a law on digital tools and processes in company law is planned for December 2026. What remains is full transposition of these rules, with company formation and filings fully online through the new register. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is improving. Priority is Medium and tractability is High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-FMW-012 · Moldova

Supplementary pension rights of mobile workers

Chapter 2

National law is not aligned with the EU directives on supplementary pension rights, such as the acquisition and preservation of rights for workers who move between Member States.

→Direction of travel Persistent Validated
■Unresolved gap Open Validated
▽Priority Low Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

The EU requirement is that workers who move between Member States can acquire and preserve their supplementary pension rights. The Commission finds that these EU rules are not incorporated into Moldovan law, and that Moldova has no occupational pension scheme, with voluntary private schemes supplementing public pensions. Moldova adopted Law No. 198/2020 on voluntary pension funds, but the Government states that effective implementation of the occupational pension system remains at an early stage. The Government undertakes to transpose Directive 98/49/EC fully and plans an amendment to Law No. 198/2020 for both directives. Neither is shown to have been adopted, and nothing is shown to have happened in practice. Moldova currently has no occupational supplementary pension system linked to employment, so the rules have limited practical reach. Sources disagree on how far the law is already aligned: the Government says, on the basis of the financial market regulator's conformity tables, that Moldovan law is aligned with Directive 2014/50/EU and partly transposes Directive 98/49/EC, while the Commission says the EU rules are not incorporated. The Government sources are machine translated. What remains is incorporating the EU rules on acquiring and preserving supplementary pension rights into Moldovan law in a form the Commission accepts. The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is Low and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

The finding is stated as a gap, not as a recommendation, and no key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition addresses supplementary pension rights. No Commission item in the evidence after 2024 returns to the issue, so the Commission has not yet responded to the Government's 2025 statement that the law is aligned with one directive and partly transposes the other. Access and rights of third-country workers

Chapter 2

This issue is not raised as a Chapter 2 requirement in EU material. The Commission records the residence rules and counts residence permits for work, such as 2,991 issued in 2023, and its 2023 call to register foreigners and give them access to services sits under Chapter 24 and does not concern employment. Moldova grants displaced persons from Ukraine temporary protection with the right to work, its employment agency signed cooperation agreements with partner organisations on refugee employment, and a draft law on the admission, stay and supervision of foreigners would replace Law No. 200/2010. The agency reports that 450 displaced jobseekers registered and 164 found work from January to September 2025, figures not corroborated by another source. UNHCR finds that only 29 percent of working-age refugees are in paid work, with language gaps, non-recognition of diplomas and scarce childcare as barriers, and that formal employment services remain underused. Research describes the procedure for employing foreigners as particularly bureaucratic, and foreigners residing for work or study cannot use employment services or register as unemployed. Consultation comments on the draft law note that work permits are tied to one employer and that labour inspection is not separated from immigration control. The draft law would enter into force only on 1 June 2027. The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel is persistent. Priority is Low and tractability is Medium. The issue is not raised in EU material. It concerns teaching the official language to the children of EU workers, and to EU workers and their family members, in line with Directive 77/486/EEC on the education of the children of migrant workers. The Commission's 2026 report says only that the law on free movement and residence of EU citizens aims to align with the acquis on the education of children of migrant workers, with no finding on tuition. In its 2025 accession programme, in machine-translated text, the Government states that the Ministry of Education and Research will create opportunities to learn Romanian for EU and European Economic Area citizens and their family members through the national programme for learning Romanian, and that children of EU citizens enrolled in national schools will be offered Romanian courses in their schools. A new edition of the programme for 2026 to 2028, with national Romanian language study centres, was to be drafted in 2025, and a mechanism for paying the teachers is planned. The Government adds that these actions could require additional teaching posts. All of these are plans: no source reports the new programme adopted, courses provided or funding allocated, and no outcome has been assessed. What remains, on the Government's own account, is putting in place and resourcing host-language tuition for EU workers, their family members and their children. The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel is new. Priority is Low and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

∅Direction of travel Insufficient evidence Validated

In 2023 the Commission said that legal alignment on services and professional qualifications needs to be complemented by non-legislative measures, including electronic platforms and procedures and administrative capacity. In this area that means a point of single contact giving service providers full online information and procedures, and a transparent electronic register of regulated professions and qualifications. Moldova's response so far consists of plans. Its 2025 accession programme lists reconfiguring the government public services portal to act as the point of single contact, and its qualifications framework roadmap for 2023 to 2027 includes making the National Register of Qualifications interoperable with the EU Europass database. The public services portal already works as a general single point of access to public services, but the Government describes its successor, the EVO portal, as a one-stop shop for public services in general rather than as the point of single contact for service providers. Nothing is shown to have happened yet on either measure, and the Government itself lists interoperability between national systems and EU digital platforms as a potential challenge. The Government sources are machine translated. What remains is a working point of single contact for service providers and an electronic register of regulated professions and qualifications. The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel cannot be determined (insufficient evidence). Priority is Low and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

The issue concerns aligning Moldova's national interoperability framework with the latest European Interoperability Framework and with the Interoperable Europe Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/903. It is not raised as a requirement in the Commission's reports or the Reform Agenda; the EU material is a Growth Plan support measure that includes alignment with the European Interoperability Framework. Moldova has a working legal and technical interoperability framework: Law No. 142/2018 on data exchange and interoperability obliges agencies to exchange data only through the interoperability solution, and the law and the decision on the MConnect platform are in force. The Government stated in 2025, in machine-translated text, that the national framework follows the principles of the European Interoperability Framework but that the Interoperable Europe Act is not transposed. It planned to amend Law No. 142/2018 to transpose the Act, and the start of drafting was announced on 3 February 2026. No source shows progress beyond that notice, and no outcome has been assessed. An international factsheet notes that Moldova is not yet part of the European Interoperability Framework data collection. What remains is transposition of the Interoperable Europe Act into the interoperability law and alignment of the national framework with the latest European Interoperability Framework. The unresolved gap is open and the direction of travel is insufficient evidence. Priority is Low and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

Alignment with the European Labour Authority regulation

Chapter 2

∅Direction of travel Insufficient evidence Validated

Under the Chapter 2 acquis, national law has to be aligned with Regulation (EU) 2019/1149 establishing the European Labour Authority, including the arrangements for cooperating with it, but no Commission requirement, key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on the Authority was found in the evidence. The Commission records that Moldova signed a cooperation agreement with the Authority in May 2025. The Government reports, in machine-translated documents, that the agreement was signed in Bratislava on 2 May 2025 and that Moldovan authorities then started a dialogue with the Authority on priority areas, including the Electronic Exchange of Social Security Information. The Government also states that a draft law to harmonise national legislation with the regulation is being prepared, planned for October 2026 and covering the Authority's role as mediator, and that it is strengthening the capacity of the labour ministry, the National Employment Agency and the State Labour Inspectorate to cooperate with the Authority. These are the Government's own account, no source shows the draft law adopted, and the capacity work names no specific measure. No outcome has been assessed. What remains is adopting and applying the law that aligns national legislation with the regulation, and building the capacity to cooperate with the Authority. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is insufficient evidence. Priority is Low and tractability is High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-FMW-007 · Moldova

Information and support for mobile workers on their rights

Chapter 2

There is no designated body supporting EU mobile workers in their rights and the system for informing them of their rights is weak.

↑Direction of travel Improving Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▽Priority Low Validated
▲Tractability High Validated

The EU requirement is a body that supports EU workers in their rights and informs them, and in 2023 the Commission found that Moldova had no specific body responsible for enforcing the right to free movement of workers. Moldova's Law No. 200/2025 gives the Equality Council the competence to promote, monitor and support equal treatment of EU citizens and their family members, and makes it the national contact point for cooperation with similar bodies in EU Member States. The Commission confirms that the law entered into force in March 2026. This is a designation in law, not a shown result. The steps needed to make it work are still planned: an amendment to the Equality Council law, a restructuring with more staff, training of Council and public authority staff, and information and referral measures by the General Inspectorate for Migration. The Council had filled 19 of 33 planned posts, and its anti-discrimination directorate, which handles complaints, 4 of 7. No source shows the Council at work for EU workers. The Government sources are machine translated. What remains is a body that in practice supports EU workers and informs them of their rights, with the mandate, structure and staff to do so. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is improving, legal only. Priority is Low and tractability is High. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-033 · Moldova

Low digital adoption by businesses

Technology and AI Digitalisation of government or economic activity

Digitalisation of the economy and adoption of digital technologies by small businesses remain low compared with the EU and undermine competitiveness, and EU programmes and digital innovation hubs are little used.

∅Direction of travel Insufficient evidence Validated
◧Unresolved gap Partly addressed Validated
▽Priority Low Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

Adoption of digital technologies by businesses is not an acquis requirement, and the Commission raises it only in general findings on the economy, with no key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on it. The Reform Agenda finds the share of Moldovan businesses using digital services low, which harms productivity and market reach, and the Government describes enterprise digitalisation, especially of small firms, as low, held back by lack of knowledge, high costs and slow returns. In response, the Government approved an SME digital transformation programme, Parliament ratified association to the Digital Europe Programme in May 2024, nine investment projects were approved under the Programme for Digital Innovation and Tech Start-ups 2025-2030, and Moldova's first European Digital Innovation Hub was launched in April 2026. As the Digital Europe contact point, the e-Governance Agency reports supporting about 200 institutions and companies and recording 14 applications to calls in 2025. No source gives the number of enterprises helped by the support programmes or reports the innovation hub's activity. Two outcomes were assessed, the contact point's support and the instant payments system's effect on small entrepreneurs, and for both success is insufficient evidence. The only repeated measure of business adoption, the share of enterprises making web sales, stands at 0.9% in both the Government's 2023 strategy and the baseline of its 2025 programme. What remains is wider adoption of digital technologies by small businesses and greater use of EU programmes and the new hub. The unresolved gap is partly addressed and the direction of travel is insufficient evidence. Priority is Low and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

  1. EU requirement Stated

    11 EU requirement items, 2022 to 2026.

    The Commission's wording on this issue consists of findings on digitalisation of the economy as a whole, not requirements. The 2022 Opinion noted that the IT sector had expanded noticeably from a low level, especially since the pandemic. The 2023 report found Moldova lagging behind in digitalisation. In 2024 the Commission found digitalisation slowly picking up thanks to more emphasis on e-government, digital skills and the ICT sector. In 2025 it found digitalisation advancing with better internet access and more public e-services, though with regional disparities, and noted that e-commerce and digital payments were lowering transaction costs for small entrepreneurs. The 2026 report says digitalisation continues to advance and describes Moldova as developing into a dynamic digital ecosystem. The tone has thus turned from lagging to advancing, but none of these findings measures adoption by businesses. The Reform Agenda's finding on low business use of digital services is the most specific EU statement on the issue. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

Electronic public procurement tools underused

Technology and AI Digital government and digital public services

The electronic public procurement system works, but some of its modules, such as the e-marketplace for low-value contracts and e-catalogues, are incomplete or little used by contracting authorities, and its data are not yet used for red-flag analysis.

∅Direction of travel Insufficient evidence Validated
∅Unresolved gap Insufficient evidence Validated
▽Priority Low Validated
∅Tractability Insufficient evidence Validated

The issue concerns fuller use of Moldova's electronic public procurement tools: modules such as the e-marketplace for low-value contracts and e-catalogues, and use of procurement data for red-flag analysis. No item states an EU requirement on fuller use of the existing modules or on red-flag analysis; the Commission's requirements on the MTender system concern its replacement by a new system, which is a separate issue. In 2021 the Commission found that the use of the online tender platform for COVID-19 related procurement, and the monitoring of those tenders, was a positive step towards transparency in health sector procurement, while the increased use of emergency procedures heightened the risk of favouring or disadvantaging certain economic operators. In 2023 the Commission reported a regulation obliging contracting authorities to carry out all stages of most low-value procurement through the State Registry of Public Procurement information system. The regulation is adopted, but no source reports how it is applied or how far the low-value module is used, and no outcome has been assessed. What remains is not known from the evidence held. The unresolved gap is insufficient evidence and the direction of travel is insufficient evidence. Priority is Low and tractability is insufficient evidence. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

RI-TEC-019 · Moldova

Data protection authority not consulted and its advice not followed

Technology and AI Data and data governance

The data protection authority is not systematically consulted on sector and implementing laws, its recommendations are often not implemented, and parliament does not follow up its reports.

∅Direction of travel Insufficient evidence Validated
∅Unresolved gap Insufficient evidence Validated
▽Priority Low Validated
◆Tractability Medium Validated

This issue concerns whether the data protection authority is consulted on sector and implementing laws and whether its advice is followed. It is not raised in EU material, so there is no EU requirement to compare against. The authority reports that 208 draft national normative acts and international treaties were submitted to it for review in 2025, and that for most of them it found that the proposed provisions needed to be completed, adjusted or revised to comply with the legal framework on personal data protection. Its opinions on individual drafts asked for clearer wording on personal data in a draft law and found the draft data governance law unclear on notifying the authority of requests for personal data, stressing that its legal mandate must be respected. These items show that drafts are sent to the authority and that it comments on them; no item shows whether its advice was then taken into account. What remains is to establish whether the authority's opinions are followed. The unresolved gap is insufficient evidence and the direction of travel is insufficient evidence. Priority is Low and tractability is Medium. Agent synthesis, validated at G7

Personal data protection in electoral processes weak

Technology and AI Data and data governance

The processing of personal data in elections, including biometric data and campaign use, lacks oversight and was introduced without assessing compliance or consulting the data protection authority.

No Commission document in the Moldova evidence sets a requirement on the protection of personal data in electoral processes, and the issue rests on a single civil society report. That report, published in March 2026, states that illegal surveys during the parliamentary election campaign used personal data databases without clarity on how they were obtained, who collected them and where they are stored. No source describes any measure Moldova has taken in response, and no source shows what has happened in practice beyond that one account. What remains, on the strength of that report alone, is oversight of how personal data are obtained, stored and used in election campaigns, a finding that other sources would need to confirm. Because there is no EU benchmark, no responsible institution named and only one item from one year, the assessment cannot measure the gap against what the EU requires or say how realistic progress would be. Comparators

Validated Comparator cases validated at G6b. The cases show what was tried, not what worked. Lessons are the tool's own reading across the evidence, validated by the analyst as conditional hypotheses; they are not stated by the sources.

Domestic preconditions for the European Health Insurance Card not in place

Lessons across the cases Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Three points recur. First, once a feasibility study and a plan exist, the Commission's request becomes concrete. After Montenegro's updated study and its February 2026 action plan, the Commission asked it to adapt its health information system for the card, equip its Health Insurance Fund and budget for reimbursements, all by accession. Moldova reached the same point in August 2026, when it finalised its feasibility study and approved an EHIC Action Plan, so the same three tasks are likely to follow, with the added task of building the integrated system that Montenegro already has. Second, legal recognition is not delivery. Montenegro recognises the card in its health insurance law but will introduce it only after accession, and the Commission still asks for its preconditions after the chapter was provisionally closed; whether the EU would accept such a deferral for Moldova cannot be judged from the evidence. Third, a recommendation alone did not move the position in Serbia: the Commission recorded no developments on the card in 2024, 2025 and 2026, including in the year after a key recommendation worded almost as Moldova's. Croatia adds that a secondary act fixing the card's validity, form and issuing was adopted about 18 months before accession, and that its insurer saw preparing contracted providers to treat visitors as the main test at accession.

CMP-0010

Croatia

What was done: Croatia prepared the European Health Insurance Card before its accession on 1 July 2013: a regulation on the card was adopted in December 2011, the Commission found preparations reaching completion in October 2012, and the Croatian Health Insurance Fund (HZZO) reports issuing the card in 2013 and EU visitors using it. Croatia already had a central health information system (CEZIH), migrated to new hardware in 2012, and by 2013 HZZO was issuing national health insurance cards alongside the EHIC, so the case shows the end state Moldova is working towards rather than how to build the missing preconditions. All statements of results come from HZZO's own reports.

Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Croatia shows the end state that Moldova's preparations aim at, with the health insurer issuing both the national card and the EHIC by 2013, working from a central health information system, and a secondary act fixing the card's validity, form and issuing details about 18 months before accession. Moldova's draft CNAM order on the card's technical specifications and the provisional replacement certificate is the nearest counterpart of Croatia's 2011 regulation. The case does not show how to build a national card or an integrated health information system where none exists, which is Moldova's gap.

◆Comparator relevance Medium Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

No evidence recorded for this step in this run.

CMP-0011

Montenegro

What was done: Montenegro recognises the European Health Insurance Card in its Law on compulsory health insurance but will introduce it only after accession, in wording the Commission repeats in 2024, 2025 and 2026. Asked in 2025 for a feasibility study, it updated one with 2025 data and in February 2026 adopted an action plan for social security coordination that sets out the technical and IT upgrades needed before accession. Chapter 2 was provisionally closed in June 2026, but no source in the project links the closure to the card, the card has not been issued and the Commission still asks for the health information system to be adapted.

Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Montenegro is some months ahead of Moldova on the same route, a feasibility study on public finances followed by an action plan that carries its findings; Moldova finalised its study and approved its EHIC Action Plan in August 2026. Once those were in place, the Commission's request to Montenegro became concrete: adapt the health information system for the card, equip the insurer and budget for reimbursements by accession. Moldova faces the same tasks with the added one of building an integrated system Montenegro already has. Montenegro had also recognised the card in its health insurance law before the chapter closed, while Moldova plans its law amendments for 2026; the case does not show that this recognition, or deferring the card to accession, was what the EU required.

Full comparator brief

National e-services portal limited in range and use

Lessons across the cases Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Three points recur. First, which services go online may matter more than how many. In North Macedonia use stayed low while a growing count of rarely requested services went online, and rose in the year that birth, marriage and citizenship certificates were added. Moldova's remaining gap sits among citizen services, of which 61% were digitalised by June 2026 against 82% of business services. Second, a count of services delivered does not show that they work end to end or are used. Montenegro developed 57 e-services in 2025 with Reform Agenda support, yet the Commission says their operability still needs to be improved. Moldova's own figures show the same gap: of 414 business services, 310 are counted as digitalised but 133 run fully end to end. Third, consolidation on one portal does not by itself close a digital divide or pay for upkeep. Albania offers 95% of applications for 1,257 services online, yet in 2026 the Commission asks it to address an emerging digital divide, resolve accessibility problems and plan and budget for maintaining its platforms. Moldova has decided, in a government decision known from machine translation, to strengthen access to e-services through EVO, and its Government says the cost of digitalisation exceeds its own resources.

CMP-0015

North Macedonia

What was done: North Macedonia's national e-services portal, in use since December 2019, reached 338 services by the end of August 2026, including partly available ones, and the Commission reports that its usage rate doubled from the previous year, after the most-demanded certificates went online in 2025. The rise starts from a low level of use, the rate is not defined, and the Commission links it to the new services only by saying that the two went together.

Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: in North Macedonia, use of the portal rose in the year the services citizens most often request went online, after years in which a growing count of rarely requested services left use low. Moldova's remaining gap sits in a similar place: 61% of citizen services are digitalised against 82% for businesses, and rural demand, which the Commission found low in 2025, rose significantly in 2026, including in rural areas where 118 service centres were set up to respond to persistently low demand. The case suggests ranking further digitalisation by how often citizens request a service, and testing the audit's stated causes of low use, promotion and the price of electronic against paper documents; Moldova's own strategy already proposes lower fees for digital services.

▲Comparator relevance High Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

Full comparator brief

Electronic public procurement system outdated and in need of replacement

Lessons across the cases Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Two points recur. First, a new system can itself become the problem. Montenegro's system was under implementation from January 2021, and an independent World Bank assessment, requested by the national procurement policy body, found in 2023 that it was a good start but needed substantial upgrading and that old technology limited further upgrading. The assessment's findings were then used to secure EU funds for an upgrade, but the only stated effect since is the Commission's unmeasured sentence on improved monitoring functions. Moldova received the technical specifications for its new system in September 2025 and published the call for bids in December 2025, so its technology choice is being made now. Second, a working system follows the law and grows in stages. North Macedonia's system was adapted to its new procurement law and modules were added over several years, under one responsible body, and its use is obligatory for all contracting authorities; this is the state Moldova is aiming for, not the route to it. Moldova's own problem is that MTender does not allow all the tools in its law and lacks annual planning and contract management, and contract management is not among the stages listed for North Macedonia either, so neither case gives evidence on it.

CMP-0013

Montenegro

What was done: Montenegro has had an electronic public procurement system under implementation since January 2021. An independent World Bank assessment requested by the country found in 2023 that the system was a good start but needed substantial upgrading and that old technology limited further upgrading, and the EU assigned funds for an upgrade. The Commission reports improvements to the system in each year from 2023 to 2025, but no source in the project shows that the technology limit was removed or that the system was replaced, and there is no measured result.

Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Moldova is now procuring a new system, with technical specifications received in September 2025 and a call for bids published in December 2025. Montenegro shows that a system introduced in 2021 could be judged within about two years to rest on old technology that limits upgrading, so a new system can itself become the problem Moldova is trying to leave behind. Montenegro's response was an independent diagnostic requested by the procurement policy body, which was then used to secure EU funds for an upgrade; whether the upgrade worked is not known.

◆Comparator relevance Medium Validated ◆Transferability Conditional Validated

No evidence recorded for this step in this run.

CMP-0014

North Macedonia

What was done: North Macedonia runs an integrated electronic public procurement system that the Commission describes as functioning efficiently in every report from 2021 to 2026. The portal was upgraded and adapted to a new legal framework by 2020, modules were added in stages, and an updated version was launched on 1 April 2025, with limited progress recorded on it. No source in the project says the earlier system was outdated, so this is a working system being upgraded, not an outdated one being replaced.

Lesson Agent synthesis, validated at G6b Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: North Macedonia shows the end state Moldova is aiming for, an integrated system obligatory for all contracting authorities, adapted to the procurement law and judged efficient by the Commission year after year. It does not show how to get there from an outdated system. Once Moldova's new system is working, North Macedonia's staged addition of modules and its single bureau managing the system could guide what follows; Moldova's Reform Agenda pilot already starts with essential modules.
