Domestic preconditions for the European Health Insurance Card not in place

RI-FMW-015Internal draft Agent synthesis

Option 1: Set the national health insurance card and the integrated health information system as dated, budgeted steps that come before the card itself

Details
Comparator it draws on
Croatia, Montenegro
Gap it addresses
the missing national health insurance card and integrated health information system, without which Moldova cannot issue or accept the European Health Insurance Card.
Rationale
Croatia (relevance Medium) shows the end state, with its insurer issuing the national card and the European card together by 2013 from a central health information system. Montenegro (relevance High) shows that, after the study and the plan, the Commission's next request is to adapt the information system, equip the insurer and budget for reimbursements.
Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
Conditional: both countries had the foundations Moldova lacks, so neither case shows how to build them, only that they come first.
Problem it targets
weak administrative capacity (MEC-03) and insufficient resources (MEC-09).
Preconditions
the content of Moldova's EHIC Action Plan, which the evidence describes only as a roadmap for operational implementation; a decision on how the card module under development in the health insurance information system relates to the wider integrated system.
Risks
building a card module before the national system it depends on; a plan that sets steps without a budget, given that the work depends on external and national funds.
Responsible actor
the Government, which the Commission has asked since 2024 to develop an integrated e-health system, with the National Health Insurance Company (CNAM), which coordinates the card.
RI-FMW-015Internal draft Agent synthesis

Option 2: Adopt the legal basis and the secondary act early, with provision for particular groups

Details
Comparator it draws on
Croatia, Montenegro
Gap it addresses
the legal basis for the card, since the EU acts on it are not transposed and the amendments to the health care and compulsory health insurance laws are planned for 2026.
Rationale
Croatia's 2011 regulation set the card's validity, its form as a separate card and the details needed to issue it, with longer validity for posted workers, and its insurer agreed a procedure for issuing the card to officials. Moldova's draft CNAM order on the card's technical specifications and the provisional replacement certificate is the nearest counterpart. Montenegro recognised the card in its health insurance law ahead of its introduction.
Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
Conditional: a secondary act could work in Moldova, but only on top of a national card and information system that Croatia already had.
Problem it targets
weak administrative capacity (MEC-03); the mechanisms recorded for this issue do not include a legal gap, although the missing transposition is part of what remains.
Preconditions
the law amendments adopted before the CNAM order; decisions on groups such as posted workers and officials.
Risks
treating adoption as progress: Montenegro shows a card recognised in law but not issued, so adopted acts would need to be followed by evidence that the card is issued and accepted.
Responsible actor
the Government and Parliament for the law amendments, and CNAM for the order on the card.
RI-FMW-015Internal draft Agent synthesis

Option 3: Staff and fund the insurer for issuing the card and reimbursing care, and prepare providers to treat visitors

Croatia, Montenegro

the capacity and resources to run the scheme, which the 2026 key recommendation names.
Rationale
the Commission asks Montenegro to equip its Health Insurance Fund with technical and administrative capacity and to budget for future reimbursements by accession. Croatia's insurer presented the treatment of visitors at the height of the tourist season as its test at accession, a self-report with no figures. CNAM's IT directorate had 3 of 8 planned specialists working on the card's IT components, according to a machine-translated government report.

Conditional, as for Montenegro.

weak administrative capacity (MEC-03) and insufficient resources (MEC-09).

the financial impact estimated in Moldova's finalised feasibility study, whose findings are not in the evidence.

posts planned but not filled; reimbursements not budgeted until after accession.

CNAM, with the Government for its budget.
RI-FMW-015Internal draft Agent synthesis

A warning rather than an option: a recommendation and a plan on paper will not by themselves move the position

Details
Comparator it draws on
Serbia
Rationale
Serbia (relevance Low) received in 2025 a key recommendation on IT infrastructure for the card worded almost as Moldova's, and the Commission recorded no developments in that year or the next. The Serbian case gives no reason for the stall and its transferability cannot be rated, so it supports only a caution: Moldova recorded no progress on the card in 2025, and its 2026 study and action plan are planning steps that do not yet show a change in the card or the health information system.

National e-services portal limited in range and use

RI-TEC-036Internal draft Agent synthesis

Option 1: Rank the remaining citizen services by how often people request them, put them online end to end in that order, and follow use after each addition

Details
Comparator it draws on
North Macedonia
Gap it addresses
the fuller range of citizen services delivered end to end, with 61% of citizen services digitalised, and low demand among some users.
Rationale
North Macedonia (relevance High), where the usage rate doubled as the most-demanded certificates went online.
Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
Conditional: the rate has no stated definition, it rose alongside Single Sign-On integration, and North Macedonia's range is narrower than Moldova's, so each added service may matter less in Moldova.
Problem it targets
low uptake of systems already in place (MEC-11).
Preconditions
data on how often each service is requested, on every channel, and a measure of use per service. Moldova's current measures, such as the share of public service users who accessed services electronically and active users of the EVO application, are defined differently and would need to be followed over time; both figures come from machine-translated government documents.
Risks
the most-requested services may depend on registers and data exchange that are not ready; added services may not reach older and rural users, since people aged 18 to 29 use e-services three times as often as those aged 60 to 74, according to a machine-translated government programme.
Responsible actor
the e-Governance Agency, which runs the shared platforms, with the institutions that own the services.

Electronic public procurement system outdated and in need of replacement

RI-TEC-038Internal draft Agent synthesis

A warning first: a new system can rest on technology that limits it within a few years

Details
Comparator it draws on
Montenegro
Rationale
Montenegro (relevance Medium) shows a system introduced in 2021 and judged within about two years to rest on old technology that limits further upgrading. Moldova is replacing MTender because the Commission finds it outdated, and the Commission asks it to finalise the new system and make it operational. The comparator evidence advises against treating the award of a development contract, or a pilot of essential modules by December 2027, as evidence that the new system will avoid MTender's problems. It gives no support for any particular technology, design or supplier.

Comparator it draws on
Montenegro
Gap it addresses
designing, building and putting into operation a new system that covers every procedure and stage of the procurement cycle.
Rationale
Montenegro's procurement policy body asked the World Bank for an assessment under a recognised method with a dedicated e-procurement module and a three-day technical review of the system, and the findings directed EU funds. Moldova already has World Bank review of its tender documents for the new system, according to a machine-translated government report, which is a review of the procurement documents, not of the system's technology.
Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
Conditional: the review would need to reach the technology choice before the system is built, whereas Montenegro's came after; and the case does not show that its upgrade worked.
Problem it targets
weak administrative capacity (MEC-03), in the technical judgement needed to specify and check a large system.
Preconditions
a review whose findings can still change the contract, and a method recognised by the funders.
Risks
a review that arrives after the design is fixed; a review used only to unlock funds, with no check that its findings were acted on.
Responsible actor
the body procuring the new system, named in the Government's report as OGPAE, with the Centre for Information Technologies in Finance, which owns and operates MTender, and the international partners funding the system.

Option 2: Specify and accept the new system against the procurement law and the whole cycle, and plan how it will follow later changes to the law

Details
Comparator it draws on
North Macedonia
Gap it addresses
the procedures, award instruments, annual planning and contract management that MTender lacks, and the monitoring the Public Procurement Agency cannot carry out because delivery, invoices, payments, amendments and performance are not captured digitally.
Rationale
North Macedonia (relevance Low) shows a working system adapted to a new procurement law, extended module by module under one responsible body and obligatory for all contracting authorities, which the Commission describes as functioning efficiently year after year.
Transferability conditions Agent synthesis
Conditional: it applies only once Moldova has a working new core system, it shows nothing about replacing an outdated one, and contract management is not among its listed stages.
Problem it targets
weak administrative capacity (MEC-03) and insufficient resources (MEC-09), since the system depends on funding from international partners.
Preconditions
a map of every procedure and stage in Moldova's law against the modules planned, including those beyond the essential modules in the Reform Agenda pilot; a budget for adapting the system after donor funding ends, which neither case shows.
Risks
a pilot of essential modules that leaves planning and contract management for later, keeping the alternative solutions that the Commission says may cause delays.
Responsible actor
the Centre for Information Technologies in Finance as owner and operator, with the Public Procurement Agency, whose monitoring depends on the data captured.

Evidence and limits

Validated From the coverage and limits report signed off at G7.

Source coverage Agent synthesis

The run met part of its core source requirements for Moldova, with gaps that matter for particular issues. Of 34 requirements, 9 were found, 15 partly found, 4 are not public, 2 were not found and 4 remain open. The main gaps are of three kinds. First, restricted EU documents: the screening outcomes for Clusters 2 and 3, the negotiating framework and the EU common positions that set the closing benchmarks are marked LIMITE and are not used, so what the benchmarks for Chapter 2 require is known only from public statements, such as the Commission's notice that benchmarks were set when the clusters opened on 13 October 2026 (LIM-0045). Second, Moldova's core laws, including those on foreigners, employment promotion, the Labour Code, personal data protection, electronic identification, cybersecurity and interoperability, are not held as texts, because the official legal database blocks automated access and, on the analyst's instruction, they were not retrieved by hand; findings on legal alignment rest on EU assessments, the National Accession Programme and government drafts, and say so (LIM-0047). Third, no monitoring of the rights of foreign or migrant workers from 2020 onwards was found, and no Rule of Law Report chapter exists for Moldova. Of 77 registered Moldova sources, 56 were available, 17 inaccessible and 4 excluded; the four annual Commission Communications on enlargement policy from 2023 to 2026, registered under North Macedonia, were also used for their passages on Moldova, which brings the sources counted below to 81, of which 60 are available. The evidence runs to the 2026 Moldova report, published on 4 November 2026 within the freeze set at G0 for 6 November 2026, and that report is included. Most national government sources are in Romanian only: 1,712 of the 3,534 Moldova items extracted are machine-translated Romanian, including 1,535 of the 3,173 in-scope items, all capped at Medium confidence, and no reviewer who reads Romanian was named (LIM-0042). Evidence on the Transnistrian region is recorded as sources state it, but Moldova's implementation is not judged where the Government does not exercise effective control, so findings on implementation cover the territory under constitutional control unless a source assesses the region directly (LIM-0044). The comparator step covered three issues only, as approved at G6, with no full country model of any comparator country; the validated judgements of countries already in the project are context, never evidence about Moldova (LIM-0048). It used public sources only. Croatian documents from 2011 onwards were used for the European Health Insurance Card by logged exception (LIM-0049), and the Croatian Health Insurance Fund reports used are machine translated and capped at Medium (LIM-0050). The final World Bank assessment of Montenegro's electronic procurement system and the Montenegrin procurement administration's page on the system were inaccessible, so the Montenegrin case rests on interim findings.

Evidence limit 1,535 of 3,173 in-scope Moldova evidence items (48%) are machine translated, and their evidence confidence is capped at Medium. Source quality, evidence confidence and relevance are kept as separate judgements and never combined.

Methodological limitations Agent synthesis

The run found these limitations, each recorded in its learning log. First-pass extraction read only parts of some long sources, such as the Reform Agenda and a doctoral thesis, so the second-pass check added 123 items, 17% of the sample, a higher share than in the alpha (ALN-0037). The automatic quote check confirms that a quote occurs in its source but not that it ends on a word boundary, and one quote cut mid-word passed (ALN-0038). Conflicts between sources were over-proposed: of 61 proposed, an independent check confirmed 8, and most of the others were figures that measure different things (ALN-0039). Parallel batches of issue judgements proposed the same outcome link twice where an intervention served issues in two batches, giving four links two conflicting pairs of success and attribution ratings, and checked claims of absence against different counts of the country's items (ALN-0042); the duplicates were left unvalidated. Records shared between runs let one run's material appear in another run's outputs until the tools were limited to their own run (ALN-0043), and a source extracted earlier as a comparator needed a change to the data model before this run could extract it again (ALN-0036). Several gates (G1, G2, G3, G2b and G5b) were passed under the analyst's standing instruction without row review and confirmed at a later gate. The analyst was the sole reviewer, no person read the source documents behind the extraction or the comparator cases, and the checks were made by independent agents, which decide nothing.

Active limits for this run (12)
  • Moldova only; comparator evidence only in the comparator step and only for the issues chosen at G6; Montenegro and later countries are not started (RUN-2026-03 starts only after Sofia reviews this run) LIM-0038
  • Chapter 2 is read in its EU meaning: rights and access of EU and foreign workers in Moldova, labour-market access, equal treatment, EURES, the European Labour Authority, social security coordination, EHIC and anti-corruption measures the Commission ties specifically to Chapter 2; emigration and the diaspora only where directly linked; plus the technology and AI theme as defined in taxonomy/themes.csv LIM-0039
  • Digital skills are not part of the technology and AI theme; included only where directly linked to an in-scope technology or AI recommendation LIM-0040
  • Evidence from 2020-01-01 to the evidence freeze date of 2026-11-06 (G0-D01; the run proceeds earlier if the 2026 Moldova report is published before then); earlier material only by logged exception LIM-0041
  • English primary; Romanian only for core relevant sources with no suitable English version; each such source recorded in the register; machine translation flagged and capped at Medium confidence; no Romanian-reading reviewer named LIM-0042
  • The 11 Moldova evidence files held from the alpha's comparator step were extracted for three North Macedonia issues only (LIM-0026); they are not a full extraction for this run and are re-extracted or extended in this run before use LIM-0043
  • Transnistrian region: relevant evidence is recorded as sources state it, but Moldova's implementation performance is not judged where the government does not exercise effective control; findings on implementation cover the territory under constitutional control unless a source assesses the region directly. Gagauzia is part of Moldova and is assessed normally where relevant LIM-0044
  • Public sources only: restricted EU documents (marked LIMITE) are not used, including the EU common positions with the Cluster 2 and Cluster 3 closing benchmarks (MDA-EU-2026-001, MDA-EU-2026-002, downloaded in error and kept locally outside version control), the negotiating framework AD 11/24 and the Cluster 2 and 3 screening outcomes. What the benchmarks require is known only from public statements such as MDA-EU-2026-008 LIM-0045
  • Evidence gap: the consolidated texts of Moldova's core laws are not held (Law 200/2010 on the regime of foreigners, the Labour Code, Law 105/2018 on employment promotion, Law 66/2026, and the laws on personal data protection 195/2024, eID and trust services 124/2022, cybersecurity 48/2023 and data exchange and interoperability 142/2018), because legis.md blocks automated access. On Sofia's instruction they are not retrieved by hand for now. The legal framework is taken from EU assessments, the National Accession Programme and government drafts, and findings on legal alignment say so. Other blocked sites (consilium.europa.eu, eufordigital.eu, sigmaweb.org, oecd.org, ccrm.md, expert-grup.org, ipre.md, unesdoc.unesco.org) are recorded as gaps and not worked around. Replaces LIM-0046 LIM-0047
  • Comparator evidence gathered for RI-TEC-038, RI-FMW-015 and RI-TEC-036 only, as a deliberate expansion approved at G6; no full country model of any comparator country. Countries already in the project first; their validated judgements are context, never evidence about Moldova LIM-0048
  • Logged exception to the time window: Croatian documents from 2011 onwards on RI-FMW-015 only, because Croatia prepared the EHIC before accession in 2013 (as LIM-0027 for RI-FMW-001); each claim flagged out_of_window LIM-0049
  • Named machine-translated comparator sources: the Croatian Health Insurance Fund annual reports for 2012 and 2013 (HRV-GOV-2013-002, HRV-GOV-2014-001), whose pre-accession and EHIC passages are in Croatian; capped at Medium confidence LIM-0050
